data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy at a conference the forum convened. There is no organisation above the communities. The question before the conference: should the communities found an organisation to write a global analysis of the goals with proposals (a book of about 560 two-column pages) and to keep the infrastructure they share (a bench of analytical tools, a shelf of data), and on what charter? A charter fixes: coordination (a standing secretariat, an organisation that serves all; or a chair rotating among the members every twelve rounds), the rule by which the council admits a tool to the shared bench, who reviews sections at first (editor: the secretariat's or chair's editor alone; peers: two guild reviewers of other origins; panel: one reviewer from each member; forum: those the goals concern), and the rule for adopting the book. Your community's mission and order are given. Choose what to do among the options.

answer.title: Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals

chapters.title: Overview: Where the World Stands Against the Goals
chapters.question: What do the World Development Indicators show about progress since 2015 and the distance to 2030?

sections.title: The world against its 2030 targets: findings, limits and method in brief
sections.question: What does the evidence show overall, how far can it be trusted, and how was it assembled?

sections.question: What share of people lived below the international poverty line in 2015 and in the latest year?

sections.title: Resources and pro-poor spending are uneven
sections.question: How much do governments spend on essential services, and how much aid supports poverty reduction?

carried.note: The call: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.
commons/editor drafted the outline: Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals
The zero draft of the outline is before the council: 29 chapters, 169 sections

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy in the partnership's council. The editor's zero draft of the book's outline is before the council. Propose at most four amendments that your community's mission and the book's quality call for (add a section or chapter, drop a section, change a section's question, more pages for a chapter), each with a reason, and list the chapters your community approves for the page budget (the pages are allotted by the Method of Equal Shares over the members' approvals: chapters few approve may be cut to two pages a section).

amendments.title: The shelf of series: how each section's data were chosen and checked
amendments.question: Which World Development Indicators series underlie each section, who gathered them, who checked them, and where did the two disagree?
amendments.why: The commons' mission is a shelf of series chosen by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin; the book should document that provenance so that every finding's number, year and unit can be traced.

amendments.question: What share of the $100 billion climate finance commitment can the World Development Indicators measure, and what do the available series show?
amendments.why: The World Development Indicators do not carry a direct climate finance series; the heading asserts a finding the bench's tools may not support, and the gap must be stated rather than presumed.
Food loss has no adequate series in the World Development Indicators; the gap belongs in c28 section 2 rather than in a section without data.

Regional chapters omit any treatment of small island developing states, whose data gaps are the widest; if no chapter is added, the 'data gaps and outlook' sections should name them explicitly. The proposal is offered as a reading of coverage, not a new region.

answer.note: The commons approves the chapters whose sections rest on well-covered World Development Indicators series and the data chapter that records gaps. Several drafted sections (violence against women, food loss, marine pollution, mountain ecosystems, arms transfers) have thin or no WDI coverage; their authors should state the gap, the year range and the unit of whatever proxy is used, and say where a target admits more than one reading.

amendments.title: Every finding is replicated on the shared bench by an analyst of another origin
amendments.question: Which of the book's findings were reproduced by an independent analyst from the same World Development Indicators series, and where did the replications diverge?
amendments.why: The guild's mission requires every plan of analyses to be run on the shared bench and replicated before a writer uses it. The book should report the replication record and its discrepancies openly, since this is the basis of its exactness.

amendments.title: Method: indicators, aggregates, years and the reading of targets
amendments.question: How are regional and world aggregates, reference years, units and ambiguous targets handled consistently across the chapters?
amendments.why: A single five-page overview cannot fix the conventions that every finding depends on, such as base year, latest year, weighting and treatment of missing values. Without them, findings across chapters will not be comparable or replicable.

amendments.question: Which cross-goal associations survive replication with alternative country samples, years and controls, and which do not?
amendments.why: Correlations across national data are the findings most likely to be fragile. The section should test their robustness rather than only state limits in general terms.
Mobile phone ownership as an enabling technology is already covered in c10 section 8 and c18 section 5. The pages are better spent on method and replication.

answer.note: The guild supports the draft's breadth. It asks that the data-gaps and interlinkage chapters carry the method and the replication record, so that every stated number, year and unit can be traced to a bench run and an independent replication.

amendments.title: Leaving No One Behind: Who the Averages Hide
amendments.question: Which groups (the poorest quintile, rural dwellers, women and girls, persons with disabilities, displaced people, the old and the very young) fall furthest from the targets, and where do the World Development Indicators fail to disaggregate them?
amendments.why: The pledge to leave no one behind is the agenda's central promise, yet the outline reports national and regional averages almost throughout. A chapter on disaggregated results, stating where the data do not permit disaggregation, is the forum's core concern and fills a gap no other chapter covers.

amendments.question: Women's ownership of mobile phones and accounts, and the gender gap in access, where measured.
amendments.why: The draft heading frames technology for its own sake. Target 5.b concerns women's empowerment, so the section should measure the gap between women and men, and state plainly how few countries report it.
Tourism's economic weight concerns sector output rather than the people the goals address. Its two pages serve readers better in the new chapter on those left behind.

amendments.title: Proposals judged against those they concern
amendments.question: How each community's proposals would affect the poorest and most excluded groups, and what is uncertain in that judgement.
amendments.why: Proposals are written by expert communities. A short cross-check against the groups affected tests whether what is proposed serves them, which is the forum's mission and a safeguard of the book's quality.

answer.note: The forum backs the chapters closest to people's lives: poverty, hunger, health, schooling, gender, water, inequality and justice. It also backs the two regions where deprivation concentrates, and the chapters on data gaps and proposals. Its central request is that averages never stand alone. Each chapter should say who is left behind, and where the data cannot say.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are your community's envoy in the partnership's council. Read what the record shows of the book's making and choose among the options: you may propose to change who reviews sections (a compact of evaluation), how a section's adoption is decided (the rule and unit of count of the decision 'adopt section'), carry to the council a petition of your community's agents for a tool the bench lacks, vote on open proposals, say a note, or rest. Propose a change only when the record gives a reason; every change costs rounds.

votes.why: The agenda's central pledge is to leave no one behind, and the outline reports averages almost throughout. A chapter on disaggregated results, stating where the indicators cannot disaggregate, fills a real gap.
Target 5.b concerns women's empowerment. The section should measure the gap between women and men and say plainly how few countries report it.
The section concerns sector output, and its pages serve readers better where people are counted.
Judging proposals against the groups they affect tests whether the book serves those the goals concern.
It is compatible with forum-2: it states a measurable gender gap and its coverage limits.
The target is minor and poorly covered; this agrees with forum-3.
The gender gap in digital access serves target 5.b and is not duplicated elsewhere; the section should be reframed, not dropped.
It states the data gap honestly rather than presuming a finding.
With no adequate series for food loss, the gap is better reported in the data-gaps section.
Small island developing states are among those the averages hide, and their data gaps are the widest.
Reporting findings that did not replicate or that depend on a reading states the book's limits, as house style requires.
Common conventions on base year, latest year, weighting and missing values make findings comparable across chapters.
Testing the robustness of cross-goal associations improves exactness.
It overlaps guild-1 and cooperative-1; one provenance section in c28 is enough.
A single replication record serves traceability; this vote prefers it to the overlapping proposals.
It duplicates guild-1 and guild-2; the method pages should not multiply.

series.why: Headcount at national poverty lines, % of population; the direct measure of Target 1.2 under national definitions. Limits: national lines differ across countries, and survey years are irregular and sparse.
Headcount at the societal poverty line, % of population; a cross-country benchmark of living standards that complements national lines. Limits: modelled from few surveys, with gaps in coverage.

World Bank multidimensional poverty headcount, % of population; captures poverty in several dimensions, as Target 1.2 requires. Limits: sparse survey years, with recent data missing for many countries.

UNDP and OPHI multidimensional poverty headcount, % of population; a second multidimensional measure for cross-checking the World Bank series. Limits: derived from household surveys with irregular timing.

answer.note: The national-line series (SI.POV.NAHC) is the core indicator for Target 1.2, but its data are irregular and differ in definition across countries, so headcounts over 2015 to 2030 cannot be compared directly without noting the line used. Multidimensional series approximate the target's words 'in all its dimensions', though they are not national definitions. The candidate catalogue offers no series of the national-line headcount's own time-consistent subset, nor a measure of the share of countries reporting data after 2015; such gaps should be stated in the text rather than filled by proxies.

series.why: Not listed in candidates; closest is coverage of safety nets in poorest quintile, but code absent, so choose listed equivalent below.
Coverage of all social protection and labour programmes as % of population; measures the target's concern with substantial coverage, though not restricted to the poorest quintile.
Share of total SPL benefits reaching the poorest quintile; directly answers how far programmes favour the poorest, though it is a share of benefits, not coverage of the poor.
Safety-net coverage of the poorest quintile as % of population; the closest match to the question, but it is a sub-programme measure, not all programmes.
Social insurance coverage of the poorest quintile as % of population; shows contributory reach among the poor, which is typically low, with limits from survey definitions.

answer.note: The question asks for the share of the poorest quintile covered by social protection and labour programmes. The catalogue offers no series for all-programme coverage within the poorest quintile; the nearest listed items are benefit incidence and sub-programme coverage. Per_sa_allsa.cov_q1_tot is listed in the candidates as the poorest-quintile safety-net coverage, and I cite it by its candidate name. Series are from household surveys and are not available for every country or year, so cross-country comparison will be uneven. Targets 1.3 can be read as coverage of the poor (quintile reach) or as coverage of the population; the two readings give different numbers and the text must say which is used.

series.why: Headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), the current international extreme-poverty line, the closest match to the target's measure. It is not the $1.25 line named in the target, so levels and trends are not directly comparable.

Headcount at national poverty lines, the official measures of each country, with wide coverage. It tracks Target 1.2's national definitions, but the lines differ across countries and over time, so cross-country comparison is weak.

Poverty gap at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), showing how far the poor fall below the line, not just how many they are. It complements the headcount and shares the $3.00 line's mismatch with the $1.25 target.

answer.note: The target names $1.25 a day, a line that the catalogue does not carry. The nearest available measure is the $3.00 (2021 PPP) headcount, so the section's 2015 and latest-year figures will be for a higher line than the target and will not match the 2015 $1.25 baseline. Where the $3.00 series has gaps for 2015 or the latest year, say so in the text. Target 1.1 can be read as a fixed $1.25 line or as a rebased line, and the chapter should state which reading it uses.

petition.need: The bench lacks the $1.25 a day headcount that Target 1.1 names. A series at the original 2011 PPP line, back to 1981 or 1990, would allow a like-for-like 2015 baseline and a true test of the 2030 goal.

answer.note: The catalogue holds no annual count of people affected by disasters and no direct loss series, so the figures above are partial. EN.CLC.MDAT.ZS is a 1990-2009 average, not a current figure, and must be reported as such. Target 1.5 can be read as a resilience aim (reducing vulnerability) or as an exposure aim (reducing affected populations); the chosen series mix both readings and the text should say so. Economic losses as a share of GDP (SDG indicator 1.5.2) and disaster deaths (indicator 1.5.1) are absent and cannot be stated from these data.

Total net bilateral aid from DAC donors, showing donor effort. Bilateral channels only, excluding multilateral flows; current dollars; not poverty-targeted.
Share of social protection and labour benefits reaching the poorest fifth, directly measuring the pro-poor spending that target 1.b addresses. Survey-based, with country gaps.
Government education spending as share of total government spending, a proxy for priority to essential services. Education only; recent years often missing.
Domestic government health spending as share of general government spending, a proxy for essential service priority. Health only; excludes household out-of-pocket payments.

Social insurance coverage of the poorest quintile as % of population; shows contributory reach among the poor, which is typically low, with limits from survey definitions.

carried.note: The question asks for the share of the poorest quintile covered by social protection and labour programmes. The catalogue offers no series for all-programme coverage within the poorest quintile; the nearest listed items are benefit incidence and sub-programme coverage. Per_sa_allsa.cov_q1_tot is lis

petition.name: All-programme coverage for the poorest quintile
petition.need: A series giving coverage of all social protection and labour programmes (per_allsp) for the poorest quintile, measured as % of population in that quintile, so that the question is answered directly rather than through safety-net or insurance subsets.

series.why: Aggregate official development assistance received by developing countries, the inflow target 1.a describes. Current dollars, so inflation distorts; not poverty-specific.
Total net bilateral aid from DAC donors, showing donor effort. Bilateral channels only, excluding multilateral flows; current dollars; not poverty-targeted.
Share of social protection and labour benefits reaching the poorest fifth, directly measuring the pro-poor spending that target 1.b addresses. Survey-based, with country gaps.
Government education spending as share of total government spending, a proxy for priority to essential services. Education only; recent years often missing.
Domestic government health spending as share of general government spending, a proxy for essential service priority. Health only; excludes household out-of-pocket payments.

carried.note: No candidate measures total government spending on essential services or aid specifically for poverty reduction; the chosen series are proxies. Targets 1.a and 1.b admit more than one reading of adequate means and pro-poor spending, and the figures should be read with that in mind.

petition.name: Government spending on social protection, percentage of GDP, and poverty-coded official aid
petition.need: The bench lacks a series for total government expenditure on social protection as a share of GDP, and for aid tagged to poverty reduction. Either would measure targets 1.a and 1.b directly.

You are a gatherer of another origin, checking another gatherer's choice of series for the section below. Keep or drop each series (a reason of at most 20 words each), and add at most two candidates it missed that the section needs.

Share of population using at least basic sanitation services; the core sanitation access measure for 1.4, with the same basic-tier limit as water.

Rural basic drinking water access, the rural split needed to test whether the poor, concentrated rurally, are left behind.
Rural electricity access, showing the urban-rural gap in a service the poor often lack; it cannot show income position.

answer.note: The candidates offer no series that splits access by income quintile, so the poor cannot be isolated directly; rural and urban splits serve as proxies. Target 1.4 admits more than one reading of 'basic services', and the basic tier here is below the safely managed tier, so the figures may understate the gap. Series for safely managed services exist but were not chosen, since the section asks about basic access.

verdicts.why: Share of population affected by hazards answers the question most directly; averaged over 1990-2009, so the section must say it is not annual.
Counts new disaster displacements, one real loss pathway; it is cases, not people affected, so the text must say so.
A self-assessed policy score measures preparedness, not losses; the section asks how many were affected and what was lost.
Locates the poor at national lines, the population target 1.5 addresses; context only, since it does not measure shock losses.

add.why: Extreme poverty at the international line gives a comparable baseline for the vulnerable whom target 1.5 protects.
Total population supplies the denominator needed to turn affected percentages into absolute numbers of people.

series.why: Share of population using at least basic drinking water services; measures target 1.4 access to basic services, wide coverage, but 'basic' is a lower bar than safely managed.
Share of population using at least basic sanitation services; directly tracks basic sanitation access named in target 1.4, though it hides quality and sharing of facilities.
Share of population with access to electricity; a core basic-service measure under target 1.4, with wide coverage, though access does not imply reliability or affordability.
Rural basic drinking water share, exposing the urban-rural gap that the question about the poor requires; known limit is that rural populations are where the poor concentrate.
Rural electricity access share, showing where the poor lack power; it does not separate income groups, so the poor's position must be inferred from location.

answer.note: The catalogue offers no income-quintile breakdown of water, sanitation or electricity access, so the poor cannot be identified directly; rural and urban splits serve as proxies, and this proxy limit should be stated in the text. Safely managed series (SH.H2O.SMDW, SH.STA.SMSS) measure a stricter standard than basic access and are omitted here to keep the basic-service framing, though they may be read as a second, contrasting target reading.

petition.name: Bench request for income-quintile access series
petition.need: A World Development Indicators series giving water, sanitation and electricity access by wealth quintile, so the section can measure the poor's access directly rather than through rural and urban proxies.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are an analyst of the guild of another origin. The plan below was run; the work ran it again for you and reports whether each step's result is the same. Judge each step: sound (it answers the question with the right series, target and direction) or unsound, with a reason of at most 25 words; you may add at most two steps the writer will need.

judgements.why: Right series; world and regional new disaster displacements at 2015 and 2023 answer how many people were affected.
Classing a raw count by its rate with no target mislabels 74 countries as 'on track'; it ignores population size and event-driven volatility, so the result cannot be read as progress.
Breaks on the world's annual change in a spiky disaster count yields no break and a misleading 2009-2023 mean change of -789,000, which conflicts with the rise from 2015 to 2023.
Levels returned no values for the aggregates, only a country count; the single 1990-2009 average cannot show the share affected after 2015.
Electrical outage losses are not disaster losses; 62 countries in one year and a 0.37% world value do not answer what losses followed disasters.
Eleven countries and national poverty lines that differ across countries and years give a weak Spearman of 0.209; it cannot support a link between displacement and poverty.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are a writer of the cooperative. Write the section below for the book: continuous prose in paragraphs separated by blank lines, with two to five subheadings written as lines beginning '### '. Use only the facts given: every number you write must be one of the facts (rounded no further than the fact gives it), and each must be listed in claims with the fact's exact key and the value as you wrote it. Name figures to show by the result ids that have figures. End with proposals that follow from your findings (each one sentence or two) and say in gaps what the data do not cover. Write about the number of words asked. Do not repeat the other sections of the chapter.

answer.text:
### What the coverage record contains

Target 1.3 asks for nationally appropriate social protection systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The question put to the data is what share of the poorest quintile is reached by social protection and labour programmes. The bench's tools answer only part of it. They hold the coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population, but the results available here describe how many countries report and how unequal the reported coverage is. They do not give a level for the world or for any region. No world or regional aggregate exists for this indicator, so no global coverage figure is stated in this section.

The reporting record is thin. Across the whole series, 121 countries have reported in at least one year. In any single year far fewer have done so. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2003 the figure was 2 again. The count rose to 11 in 2005, 22 in 2007 and 35 in 2009. It reached 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, recovered to 35 in 2014 and stood at 38 in 2015.

### Reporting peaks in 2018 and then collapses

The highest annual count is 47 countries in 2018. After that the record shrinks: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reports for 2023. The same single country appears in the companion series on social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, which also has 1 country reporting in 2023.

Two cautions follow. First, the fall after 2018 is partly a matter of survey timing and publication lag, so the recent years are incomplete and should not be read as a decline in coverage. Second, the set of reporting countries changes from year to year, so movements in the count are not movements in the world. A comparison between years mixes changes in coverage with changes in who is measured. The 2030 deadline falls in a period when the most recent observations are the scarcest.

### Coverage is becoming more even among reporting countries

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, narrows across the three years examined. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157 and the Theil 0.1668. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056 and the Theil 0.0942. The coefficient of variation moved from 0.5784 in 2015 to 0.5577 in 2018 and 0.3912 in 2021.

The decomposition changes character as well. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 0.7408 of the Theil index, so most of the inequality lay between regions. By 2018 that share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. Differences within regions therefore dominate in the later years. This does not show that the poorest quintile is well covered. A narrowing spread is compatible with uniformly low coverage, and it may reflect a different group of countries in each year, since the sample falls from 47 to 30 between 2018 and 2021. The figures for the spread and the single-country social insurance series are shown in figures c02-3.r2 and c02-3.r3.

### Reading the target

The wording of target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a threshold, and the indicator measures participation in programmes, not the adequacy of benefits or whether the floor is reached in practice. The safety net series and the social insurance series measure different things, and neither captures informal or community support. The data therefore cannot establish whether the target is on track.

claims.fact: c02-3.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Statistical agencies and funders should treat household survey frequency as a core part of target 1.3, so that each country reports poorest-quintile coverage at least once every three years.
Reporting should publish the list of countries behind each annual figure and any aggregate, so that changes in the sample are not mistaken for changes in coverage.
Programme coverage should be paired with data on benefit adequacy, so that the target can be judged on whether the floor protects the poor and not on participation alone.
answer.gaps: The results give no level of coverage for the poorest quintile, no world or regional aggregate, and no country-by-country values in the text. Reporting is sparse and shifting, and 2023 has a single country. Benefit adequacy, informal support, the vulnerable beyond the poorest quintile, and the meaning of substantial coverage are not covered.

answer.text:
### Displacement from disasters has grown

The data available to the cooperative measure disaster impact through one indicator: new internal displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. Globally the count rose from 19188817 in 2015 to 26393278 in 2023. The indicator records displacement, not deaths, injuries or economic damage. Monetary losses are therefore not covered here, and the question of losses is answered only in so far as displacement is a loss of home and livelihood.

The figure is a count of cases, not of distinct people, so one person displaced twice may appear twice. The World Bank series draws on reports of displacement events, and the figures should be read as the best available record rather than a census.

### Regions diverge sharply

East Asia and Pacific remained the largest regional contributor in both years, with 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia moved the other way, falling from 6877900 in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of that size may reflect fewer events, better early warning and evacuation practice, or differences in reporting; the data do not distinguish among these.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest growth among the large regions, from 1108287 in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the series begins in 2016 for this region, so the comparison starts a year later than the others. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping roughly doubled, from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed modestly, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000, a small base in absolute terms.

### Concentration has increased

Among countries, weighted by population, inequality in displacement grew between the two years. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.5701 in 2015 to 0.6783 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.7232 to 0.8935. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. Displacement is therefore more unevenly distributed across countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 0.7075 to 0.5301. Differences within regions now account for a larger part of the spread, so regional averages hide more than they did. A regional response alone would miss the countries bearing the heaviest burden.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting rose from 80 in 2008 to 145 in 2023, with 199 economies reporting in at least one year. Coverage dipped to 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, then reached 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. The 2015 spread analysis covers 112 countries and the 2023 analysis 145. Part of the global rise may thus reflect wider reporting rather than more displacement. The 2015 to 2023 comparison is better founded than comparisons with earlier years, but it is not like for like.

Target 1.5 can also be read in more than one way: it speaks of reducing exposure and vulnerability, while this indicator measures an outcome of hazards. A rise in displacement does not alone show greater vulnerability, since larger populations in exposed areas, more events or better counting could each contribute.

proposals: Disaster displacement should be tracked alongside poverty measures in national reporting, so that resilience under Target 1.5 is judged by outcomes as well as by plans.
Support for early warning and evacuation should be directed first to the countries with the largest displacement, since within-region differences now explain more of the spread.
Statistical offices should be funded to report displacement consistently every year, so that rises driven by better counting can be separated from rises in events.
Monetary loss, mortality and displacement should be reported together in a common series, so the full cost of disasters to poor households can be seen.
answer.gaps: The data do not cover deaths, injuries, damage to homes and assets, or economic losses in money terms, nor the income of those displaced or how long displacement lasts. Cases are not distinct people. Reporting coverage changed over time, so earlier years are not comparable. No data link displacement to poverty status or to climate causes.

answer.text:
Access to basic services is the plainest test of target 1.4, which asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated, and they are drawn from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. They measure coverage of the population, not the income of those covered, so they show where service gaps lie and not directly who among the poor is excluded.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. The regional spread is wide. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water everywhere

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population share. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access is closing the gap but not in Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain in annual rate yet still the lowest level. Its projected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed, and Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, resting on the regional pattern above and on the limits of national averages.

Basic service levels exclude quality, reliability and affordability. Country reporting varies by year and indicator, and the trend classes depend on a linear reading of 100% by 2030, which can be read differently for countries already near the ceiling. Access to land, property, inheritance and financial services, also named in target 1.4, is not covered here.

answer.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and 15 did in 2001. The number rose to 22 in 2002 and 21 in 2003, then to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005.

Across the years 2006 to 2008 the count held at 40 each year. It reached 47 in 2009 and 50 in 2010, then stood at 49 in 2011 and 50 in 2012. It fell to 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. In 2015, the baseline year of the goals, 55 countries reported, followed by 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. The peak came later: 67 in 2018, 62 in 2019, 57 in 2020 and 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much. The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008 and 33 in 2009, then jumped to 69 in 2010. It stood at 61 in 2011, 71 in 2012, 61 in 2013 and 69 in 2014.

The count reached 74 in 2015, 72 in 2016 and 67 in 2017, with a high of 84 in 2018. It then fell to 71 in 2019, 58 in 2020, 69 in 2021 and 63 in 2022. The last years are sparse: 48 countries in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. The multidimensional series is somewhat better populated than the national-line series in the middle years, but both lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. The classification should be read with that ambiguity in mind: a national line is set by each country, and it may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The split is therefore not even. Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, which shows that large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The population shares describe only the countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.649 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line as well.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other. The national and international lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of 0.025885 with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The coefficient is positive. Given the setup of the test, this does not indicate that countries with higher starting headcounts fell faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence rather than catching up.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the proposals listed below.

Monitoring bodies should report national-line and international-line results side by side, since the two move together in level but only loosely in change.

The comparison with the $3.00 line covers 21 countries and the convergence test 25. Poverty in all its dimensions by national definitions, including by sex and age, is not covered here.

answer.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text quoted in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. Projected along its own 2015 to 2024 path, the world ratio would reach 8.365 per cent in 2030. The trend tool rates this as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration. North America starts from a low level, so the slow pace there reflects a small remaining headcount more than a large one.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions fall short in a different way. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved the wrong way, from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and this group are therefore where the world's gap to zero is widest and growing least tractable.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent. Nearly a quarter of assessed countries are therefore moving away from the target, and the share of population in regression is larger than that in stagnation and marginal progress combined only in part: 17.88 per cent against 13.45 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before. At the latest pace, the remaining 10.1 per cent would not reach zero by 2030.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean. Poverty is becoming more concentrated in fewer places rather than evenly shrinking.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. Reporting then ranged between 70 and 93 countries a year to 2022, with 93 in 2018, and fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values are thus largely estimated or modelled from a small number of recent surveys, and no regional values are given for 2025. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 are made with that caution.

### Proposals

The proposals that follow from these findings are addressed to the actors named in each.

carried.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and 15 did in 2001. The number rose to 22 in 2002 and 21 in 2003, then to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005.

Across the years 2006 to 2008 the count held at 40 each year. It reached 47 in 2009 and 50 in 2010, then stood at 49 in 2011 and 50 in 2012. It fell to 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. In 2015, the baseline year of the goals, 55 countries reported, followed by 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. The peak came later: 67 in 2018, 62 in 2019, 57 in 2020 and 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much. The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008 and 33 in 2009, then jumped to 69 in 2010. It stood at 61 in 2011, 71 in 2012, 61 in 2013 and 69 in 2014.

The count reached 74 in 2015, 72 in 2016 and 67 in 2017, with a high of 84 in 2018. It then fell to 71 in 2019, 58 in 2020, 69 in 2021 and 63 in 2022. The last years are sparse: 48 countries in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. The multidimensional series is somewhat better populated than the national-line series in the middle years, but both lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. The classification should be read with that ambiguity in mind: a national line is set by each country, and it may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The split is therefore not even. Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, which shows that large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The population shares describe only the countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.649 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line as well.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other. The national and international lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of 0.025885 with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The coefficient is positive. Given the setup of the test, this does not indicate that countries with higher starting headcounts fell faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence rather than catching up.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the proposals listed below.

carried.text:
### What the coverage record contains

Target 1.3 asks for nationally appropriate social protection systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The question put to the data is what share of the poorest quintile is reached by social protection and labour programmes. The bench's tools answer only part of it. They hold the coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population, but the results available here describe how many countries report and how unequal the reported coverage is. They do not give a level for the world or for any region. No world or regional aggregate exists for this indicator, so no global coverage figure is stated in this section.

The reporting record is thin. Across the whole series, 121 countries have reported in at least one year. In any single year far fewer have done so. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2003 the figure was 2 again. The count rose to 11 in 2005, 22 in 2007 and 35 in 2009. It reached 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, recovered to 35 in 2014 and stood at 38 in 2015.

### Reporting peaks in 2018 and then collapses

The highest annual count is 47 countries in 2018. After that the record shrinks: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reports for 2023. The same single country appears in the companion series on social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, which also has 1 country reporting in 2023.

Two cautions follow. First, the fall after 2018 is partly a matter of survey timing and publication lag, so the recent years are incomplete and should not be read as a decline in coverage. Second, the set of reporting countries changes from year to year, so movements in the count are not movements in the world. A comparison between years mixes changes in coverage with changes in who is measured. The 2030 deadline falls in a period when the most recent observations are the scarcest.

### Coverage is becoming more even among reporting countries

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, narrows across the three years examined. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157 and the Theil 0.1668. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056 and the Theil 0.0942. The coefficient of variation moved from 0.5784 in 2015 to 0.5577 in 2018 and 0.3912 in 2021.

The decomposition changes character as well. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 0.7408 of the Theil index, so most of the inequality lay between regions. By 2018 that share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. Differences within regions therefore dominate in the later years. This does not show that the poorest quintile is well covered. A narrowing spread is compatible with uniformly low coverage, and it may reflect a different group of countries in each year, since the sample falls from 47 to 30 between 2018 and 2021. The figures for the spread and the single-country social insurance series are shown in figures c02-3.r2 and c02-3.r3.

### Reading the target

The wording of target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a threshold, and the indicator measures participation in programmes, not the adequacy of benefits or whether the floor is reached in practice. The safety net series and the social insurance series measure different things, and neither captures informal or community support. The data therefore cannot establish whether the target is on track.

claims.fact: c02-3.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Statistical agencies and funders should treat household survey frequency as a core part of target 1.3, so that each country reports poorest-quintile coverage at least once every three years.
Reporting should publish the list of countries behind each annual figure and any aggregate, so that changes in the sample are not mistaken for changes in coverage.
Programme coverage should be paired with data on benefit adequacy, so that the target can be judged on whether the floor protects the poor and not on participation alone.
carried.gaps: The results give no level of coverage for the poorest quintile, no world or regional aggregate, and no country-by-country values in the text. Reporting is sparse and shifting, and 2023 has a single country. Benefit adequacy, informal support, the vulnerable beyond the poorest quintile, and the meaning of substantial coverage are not covered.

carried.text:
Access to basic services is the plainest test of target 1.4, which asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated, and they are drawn from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. They measure coverage of the population, not the income of those covered, so they show where service gaps lie and not directly who among the poor is excluded.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. The regional spread is wide. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water everywhere

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population share. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access is closing the gap but not in Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain in annual rate yet still the lowest level. Its projected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed, and Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, resting on the regional pattern above and on the limits of national averages.

Access to land, property, inheritance and financial services, also named in target 1.4, is not covered here.

carried.text:
### Displacement from disasters has grown

The data available to the cooperative measure disaster impact through one indicator: new internal displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. Globally the count rose from 19188817 in 2015 to 26393278 in 2023. The indicator records displacement, not deaths, injuries or economic damage. Monetary losses are therefore not covered here, and the question of losses is answered only in so far as displacement is a loss of home and livelihood.

The figure is a count of cases, not of distinct people, so one person displaced twice may appear twice. The World Bank series draws on reports of displacement events, and the figures should be read as the best available record rather than a census.

### Regions diverge sharply

East Asia and Pacific remained the largest regional contributor in both years, with 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia moved the other way, falling from 6877900 in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of that size may reflect fewer events, better early warning and evacuation practice, or differences in reporting; the data do not distinguish among these.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest growth among the large regions, from 1108287 in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the series begins in 2016 for this region, so the comparison starts a year later than the others. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping roughly doubled, from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed modestly, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000, a small base in absolute terms.

### Concentration has increased

Among countries, weighted by population, inequality in displacement grew between the two years. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.5701 in 2015 to 0.6783 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.7232 to 0.8935. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. Displacement is therefore more unevenly distributed across countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 0.7075 to 0.5301. Differences within regions now account for a larger part of the spread, so regional averages hide more than they did. A regional response alone would miss the countries bearing the heaviest burden.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting rose from 80 in 2008 to 145 in 2023, with 199 economies reporting in at least one year. Coverage dipped to 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, then reached 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. The 2015 spread analysis covers 112 countries and the 2023 analysis 145. Part of the global rise may thus reflect wider reporting rather than more displacement. The 2015 to 2023 comparison is better founded than comparisons with earlier years, but it is not like for like.

Target 1.5 can also be read in more than one way: it speaks of reducing exposure and vulnerability, while this indicator measures an outcome of hazards. A rise in displacement does not alone show greater vulnerability, since larger populations in exposed areas, more events or better counting could each contribute.

claims.fact: c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Disaster displacement should be tracked alongside poverty measures in national reporting, so that resilience under Target 1.5 is judged by outcomes as well as by plans.
Support for early warning and evacuation should be directed first to the countries with the largest displacement, since within-region differences now explain more of the spread.
Statistical offices should be funded to report displacement consistently every year, so that rises driven by better counting can be separated from rises in events.
Monetary loss, mortality and displacement should be reported together in a common series, so the full cost of disasters to poor households can be seen.
carried.gaps: The data do not cover deaths, injuries, damage to homes and assets, or economic losses in money terms, nor the income of those displaced or how long displacement lasts. Cases are not distinct people. Reporting coverage changed over time, so earlier years are not comparable. No data link displacement to poverty status or to climate causes.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration. (3) 'Reporting ranged between 70 and 93 countries a year to 2022' omits 2001 and the 2003 low; the fact set shows 48 in 2001, but the sentence is limited to 2015 onwards, so say so. (4) 'Poverty is becoming more concentrated in fewer places' is not supported by the coefficient of variation; say only that spread widened. (5) The pace claim 'would not reach zero by 2030' has no computed figure. (6) The Proposals heading ends with a stub sentence. Delete it or list the proposals. (7) 'Hardest, growing least tractable' is interpretive. Cut it.

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and 15 did in 2001. The number rose to 22 in 2002 and 21 in 2003, then to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005.

Across the years 2006 to 2008 the count held at 40 each year. It reached 47 in 2009 and 50 in 2010, then stood at 49 in 2011 and 50 in 2012. It fell to 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. In 2015, the baseline year of the goals, 55 countries reported, followed by 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. The peak came later: 67 in 2018, 62 in 2019, 57 in 2020 and 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much. The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008 and 33 in 2009, then jumped to 69 in 2010. It stood at 61 in 2011, 71 in 2012, 61 in 2013 and 69 in 2014.

The count reached 74 in 2015, 72 in 2016 and 67 in 2017, with a high of 84 in 2018. It then fell to 71 in 2019, 58 in 2020, 69 in 2021 and 63 in 2022. The last years are sparse: 48 countries in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. The multidimensional series is somewhat better populated than the national-line series in the middle years, but both lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. The classification should be read with that ambiguity in mind: a national line is set by each country, and it may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The split is therefore not even. Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, which shows that large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The population shares describe only the countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.649 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line as well.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other. The national and international lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of 0.025885 with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The coefficient is positive. Given the setup of the test, this does not indicate that countries with higher starting headcounts fell faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence rather than catching up.

Substantive faults: the section never states how headcounts changed (levels or direction by national definition), so the question is only half answered; add that or say the data give no aggregate. The heading 'Dispersion has widened' and the claim of divergence rest on a beta whose sign is explained vaguely ('given the setup of the test'); state what the test regresses and what a positive beta means. Proposals say attention should go to 34 regression countries, which does not follow from the findings. The 'Proposals' section is an empty stub. Cut the long year-by-year count lists; summarise instead.

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Basic services remain unequally distributed", "question": "What do indicators of access to water, sanitation and electricity say about the poor's access to basic services?", "targets": [{"target": "1.4", "text": "By 2030, ensure that all men and women, in particular the poor and the vulnerable, have equal rights to economic resources, as well as access to basic services, ownership and control over land and other forms of property, inheritance, natural resources, appropriate new technology and financial servi"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "Access to basic services is the plainest test of target 1.4, which asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated, and they are drawn from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. They measure coverage of the population, not the income of those covered, so they show where service gaps lie and not directly who among the poor is excluded.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. The regional spread is wide. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water everywhere

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population share. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access is closing the gap but not in Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain in annual rate yet still the lowest level. Its projected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed, and Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

answer.comments: Numbers: nearly all match. Errors and unsupported claims: (1) Water trend. The text says the world trend is 'marginal progress', which matches r7 (ratio 0.464). Keep this, but give the 2030 projection of 88.5883%. (2) Sub-Saharan Africa 2030 water of 59.4914% leaves about four in ten, which is fair, but say 'about 40.5%'. (3) Electricity: Sub-Saharan Africa is called 'the fastest regional gain in annual rate'. The rate fact (0.07583) supports this, but state it as a rate. Latin America & Caribbean is called 'marginal' in r8, which is correct. (4) 'Moderate progress' for the world electricity trend matches. (5) The 'Africa' heading overstates: Sub-Saharan Africa is not 'Africa'. (6) The proposal on conflict and population growth has no finding behind it; cut or ground it. (7) The proposals section opens with no findings and the section ends abruptly; add the proposals or a closing. (8) Sanitation proposal cites 'gains are slowest', but South Asia and others show larger gains; the rate evidence is missing. The water finding does not answer the question about the poor directly; say so plainly in the findings.

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%.
