Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, so the data given here do not support a statement of how the headcount changed worldwide. Change can be described only country by country, as in the next section.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Shares below are given to one decimal place.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 regresses each country's change in headcount on its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The positive sign means that higher starting headcounts were associated with larger increases or smaller falls, not catching up.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence, though the group is small and may not represent all countries.

answer.comments: Numbers: the 3.8% share for moderate progress should be 3.76%, so 3.8% is a rounding of 0.0376, and 26.0% for regression is 25.96%, also a rounding. The text says shares are given to one decimal place, which is stated, so this is acceptable, but 63.8%, 4.4% and 2.1% match. Check that rounded values are flagged. Other numbers match their facts. Problems: (1) The question asks how headcounts changed; the section gives no country-level change, only coverage, trend classes and the convergence test. Add the direction of change or state plainly that it cannot be given. (2) The text says 'the next section' will describe country change, but none does; cut or fix. (3) The 'Dispersion has widened' heading overstates a 25-country result. (4) Beta is called positive 'larger increases or smaller falls' without data on direction; keep hedged. (5) The Proposals section opens with a stub sentence; the proposals are not tied to findings. Link each to its finding. The proposal for a two-year publication limit has no supporting finding on lags.

They therefore show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show directly whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is also classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914%, which leaves about 40.5% of its rural population without basic water if the present pace holds.

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, the lowest level of any region. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met. The share of the assessed population in these is 46.64%. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered. They therefore show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show directly whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is also classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914%, which leaves about 40.5% of its rural population without basic water if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, the lowest level of any region. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 sanitation value for the regions is available among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged here from levels alone.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met. The share of the assessed population in these is 46.64%. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access closes the gap except in Sub-Saharan Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%. Its annual rate of 0.07583 is the highest of any region, yet it is still classed as marginal progress, and the expected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

data.prompt: {"tool": "latest-year-survey-coverage", "need": "Counts of countries with a survey-based poverty estimate dated 2023 or later, by region, to separate observed from modelled values.", "shelf examples": ["SH.DYN.MORT", "SI.POV.DDAY", "SP.POP.TOTL"]}

answer.about: Counts, by region, the countries whose latest available value for a series is dated at or after a cutoff year, as a proxy for recent survey coverage. Poverty headcount values exist only in survey years, so a recent date indicates an observed rather than modelled estimate; for modelled series the proxy does not hold.

params.name: series
params.meaning: World Bank WDI series code, for example SI.POV.DDAY

params.name: cutoff_year
params.meaning: Earliest year counted as recent, for example 2023

cases.expect: Small number of countries with a value dated 2023 or later, far fewer than the countries with any estimate; regional counts sum to the recent total and share_recent_percent is low.

Nearly every country has a value dated 2023 or later, so share_recent_percent is close to 100 and regional recent counts nearly equal with_data counts, showing the contrast with survey-based poverty data.

data.prompt: {"tool": "coverage-and-recency-indicator-for-natio", "need": "A series giving, for each year from 2015, the number of countries with a national-line poverty estimate and the survey year used, so that missing data and a target read in more than one way (national lines versus multidimensional measures) can be reported exactly.", "shelf examples": ["SH.DYN.MORT", "SI.POV.DDAY", "SP.POP.TOTL"]}

answer.about: Counts, for each year in a window starting 2015, how many countries have a value in a chosen series, and reports how recent each country's latest survey year is. Intended for national-line poverty series so that missing data can be stated exactly. Aggregates are excluded by using only codes present in the region map.

params.name: series
params.meaning: World Bank series code to examine, for example SI.POV.DDAY

params.name: start_year
params.meaning: First year of the window, default 2015

params.name: end_year
params.meaning: Last year of the window, default 2022

cases.expect: Facts give a country count for each year 2015 to 2022, all well below the number of countries in scope because survey data are sparse; countries_with_any_estimate is smaller than countries_in_scope; median_latest_year lies within 2015 to 2022.
Population is nearly complete: each year 2015 to 2020 has a count close to countries_in_scope, coverage_share_pct is near 100, and median_latest_year is 2020.

### Education spending has moved little at the global level

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, and regional movements differ in direction and size. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

Two regions with high shares show different paths. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. The end years differ by region, and the start year is 2016 for one region, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they cannot show whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need; they show only the size of the gap in budget share.

Coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid has grown in every region reported

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan had the largest proportional rise, from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493, which is about 81 per cent by the cooperative's own calculation from these two figures.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America's series is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, and is no meaningful comparator. Regional shares are not given in the results, so no claim is made here about concentration beyond the ranking of amounts. The figures are in current dollars, so part of the growth reflects prices, and the series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. carried.text:
### Education spending has moved little at the global level

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, and regional movements differ in direction and size. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

Two regions with high shares show different paths. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. The end years differ by region, and the start year is 2016 for one region, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they cannot show whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need; they show only the size of the gap in budget share.

Coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid has grown in every region reported

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan had the largest proportional rise, from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493, which is about 81 per cent by the cooperative's own calculation from these two figures.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America's series is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, and is no meaningful comparator. Regional shares are not given in the results, so no claim is made here about concentration beyond the ranking of amounts. The figures are in current dollars, so part of the growth reflects prices, and the series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

carried.comments: Numbers check against the facts, with these exceptions. 'About 40.5%' for Sub-Saharan Africa is derived (100 minus 59.4914), not a fact, so state it as 40.5086 or cut it. The Sub-Saharan Africa sanitation 'lowest level of any region' and 'largest gain' for South Asia are comparisons not backed by cited facts; South Asia's gain (29.39 points) is correct, but say so plainly. The text says Latin America & Caribbean is 'marginal' for electricity, which matches. Proposal 1 claims 'every projected 2030 value' falls short, yet no sanitation projection exists; the text itself says so. Restrict it to water (59.4914%) and electricity (55.3497%). The final section 'Proposals follow from the gaps' lists no actual proposals and is thin; state them or cut the heading. The section answers the question only by regional rural averages; say that the poor are not separately identified in the findings' first paragraph, which is done, but add urban absence earlier.

Most numbers match their facts. Problems to correct:

1. The text says the 2015-2024 world path gives 8.365 per cent in 2030, but the fact is simply the expected 2030 value. Do not add an unsupported description of the path.

2. The text says Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East group 'fall short' and adds that 'North America starts from a low level, so the slow pace reflects a small remaining headcount'. The data give no such cause; cut it or mark it as interpretation. The statement 'Each period is slower than the one before' is derived and is fine.

3. The proposal to prioritise surveys in countries with 'oldest or missing data' has no finding about old data; only the falling count of reporters. Reword to match it.

4. The proposal for regression countries asks governments to explain why poverty rises, though the gaps say no causes are given; soften.

5. Cut the empty 'Proposals' lead-in line.

Numbers: the 3.8% share for moderate progress should be 3.76%, so 3.8% is a rounding of 0.0376, and 26.0% for regression is 25.96%, also a rounding. The text says shares are given to one decimal place, which is stated, so this is acceptable, but 63.8%, 4.4% and 2.1% match. Check that rounded values are flagged. Other numbers match their facts. Problems: (1) The question asks how headcounts changed; the section gives no country-level change, only coverage, trend classes and the convergence test. Add the direction of change or state plainly that it cannot be given. (2) The text says 'the next section' will describe country change, but none does; cut or fix. (3) The 'Dispersion has widened' heading overstates a 25-country result. (4) Beta is called positive 'larger increases or smaller falls' without data on direction; keep hedged. (5) The Proposals section opens with a stub sentence; the proposals are not tied to findings. Link each to its finding. The proposal for a two-year publication limit has no supporting finding on lags.

Numbers match the facts, but derived figures and some claims do not. (1) 'About 40.5%' for Sub-Saharan Africa is not a cited fact (100 minus 59.4914 is 40.5086); cite it or drop it. (2) 'Annual rate of 0.07583 is the highest of any region' is unsupported: no other region's electricity rate is shown, and the unit is unstated. (3) The heading 'closes the gap except in Sub-Saharan Africa' overlooks Latin America & Caribbean, classed marginal. (4) The proposal says 'every projected 2030 value falls well short of 100%' but no 2030 sanitation projection exists, as the text admits; restrict it to water and electricity. (5) The proposals section opens with an empty sentence and lacks a finding on the 39 regressing countries tied to a stated year. (6) Say that the sanitation indicator's regression share covers population, not rural population. (7) The question concerns the poor; state more plainly that rural coverage is only a proxy.

Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot yet answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile. No regional or world aggregate is available for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

Coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, measured as a percentage of that quintile, rests on household surveys. Survey timing therefore sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000 two countries reported, and in 2002 three. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, a drop that reflects survey cycles rather than any change in policy. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count declined: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only one country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The figure shows that the indicator has some historical reach, but in any single year fewer than half of those countries are observed. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was measured for three years. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini fell to 0.2056, the Theil index to 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation to 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality changes sharply

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a larger shift. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index, expressed in the data as 0.7408. By 2018 the between-region share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. By 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region.

The change is large enough to suggest that the composition of the sample, not only the policies of governments, drives the result. Regions represented by few countries in 2015 may have been better represented later, which would shift the weight from the between-region to the within-region component. The data given here do not allow that explanation to be tested.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only one country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world. Social insurance, which includes contributory pensions and unemployment benefits, is the kind of protection that often misses people in informal work, but the data here cannot show whether that is so.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding for this section is therefore about the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse, irregular and declining in recent reporting.

answer.text:
The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate is available for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

Coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, measured as a percentage of that quintile, rests on household surveys. Survey timing therefore sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000 two countries reported, and in 2002 three. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013. The results do not say why the count fell, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count fell: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only one country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was measured for three years. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality falls

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a marked change. In 2015, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index. By 2018 the between-region share was 28.8 per cent, and by 2021 it was 21.4 per cent. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. In 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region.

The size of the change suggests that the composition of the sample, and not only government policy, may drive the result. The data given here do not allow that explanation to be tested.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only one country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding for this section concerns the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse and irregular, and the count of reporting countries is lower in 2022 and 2023 than in 2018.

proposals: Survey programmes should be scheduled so that a stable set of countries reports coverage of the poorest quintile at regular intervals, allowing a true panel rather than a shifting sample.
Target 1.3 should be accompanied by a stated numerical threshold for substantial coverage, so that reported figures can be judged against it.
Reports of the spread of coverage should state the number and identity of countries observed in each year, so that narrowing dispersion is not mistaken for convergence.

Reporting countries differ between years, so trends cannot be separated from sample change. Social insurance coverage is observed for one country in 2023. The indicator excludes the vulnerable beyond the poorest fifth and programmes that surveys do not capture. The reasons for changes in the number of reporting countries are not in the results.

answer.text:
### Displacement as the measure of disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built, and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced. The World Development Indicators offer one series that bears directly on exposure: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. The series counts displacement events, not distinct people, so one person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It also says nothing about income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Losses in money, lives or livelihoods are not measured by it. The question of how many people were affected, and what losses followed, can therefore be answered only in part, through displacement.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19188817 cases in 2015 and reached 26393278 cases in 2023. The increase over the period is substantial, but the two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because disaster displacement varies sharply from year to year with the severity of storms, floods and other events. A further caution applies to the comparison: the number of reporting countries changed over the period, as the next section shows.

### Regional contrasts

The regional picture diverges more than the global total suggests. East Asia and Pacific recorded 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023, and remains the largest regional source of new displacement in both years. South Asia moved in the opposite direction, from 6877900 cases in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of this size is more likely to reflect the particular events of the two years than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1108287 cases in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 cases in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because the figure for 2015 is not given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1212730 cases in 2015 to 2481660 in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These regional movements matter for the target because the regions where displacement has grown most quickly include some with large populations living in poverty. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the ones displaced, only that exposure to displacing events grew most where the regional counts rose most.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed greatly. It was 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009, and stood at 73 in 2010, 62 in 2011 and 79 in 2012. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014, and reached 112 in 2015. Later figures were 116 in 2016, 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018, 136 in 2019, 142 in 2020, 133 in 2021, 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

The consequence is that part of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may be a product of wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are therefore not a like-for-like comparison. Earlier years are weaker still, and no trend should be drawn from the period before 2013.

### Concentration of displacement is increasing

Inequality among countries in displacement, weighted by population, has widened. The Gini coefficient was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893 over the same years, and the coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: displacement is more concentrated in a smaller number of countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of the Theil index that lies between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015, then, most of the inequality came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share arises from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages therefore hide more than they once did, and a response designed by region would miss a growing part of the concentration. The comparison should be read with the caution already given, as the sample grew from 112 to 145 countries.

### Proposals follow

The findings support a small number of proposals, set out below.

c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Countries that have not yet reported disaster displacement should be supported to do so on a consistent annual basis, so that trends can be separated from changes in coverage.
Disaster-risk financing and early-warning investment should be directed first to the countries where displacement is concentrated, including within regions, and not allocated by regional average.
Displacement counts should be published alongside household poverty data for the same areas, so that the exposure of the poor can be measured directly against Target 1.5.
answer.gaps: The series counts displacement cases, not distinct people, and gives no breakdown by income, so it cannot show how many poor people were affected. It does not measure deaths, damage to property, lost income or economic losses, so the losses that followed are not covered. Reporting rose from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, which limits comparison across years, and earlier years are thinly covered. Single-year values vary with the events of the year. Target 1.5 can also be read as covering shocks that are not disasters, which this series does not capture.

data.text: The book is a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, written by five communities of invented agents; it is no institution's report. Every number comes from the World Bank's World Development Indicators through the bench's tools. House style: British spelling; declarative headings, never questions; no first person; plain, exact prose; a finding states its number, its year and its unit; where data are missing or a target can be read in more than one way, say so. You are an analyst of the guild of another origin, checking a tool another built before the bench admits it. The work ran it on its declared cases; read the code and the outputs and say whether it computes what it claims (sound) or not (unsound), with a reason of at most 40 words.

data.prompt: {"tool": "headcount-ratio-at-1-25-a-day-2011-ppp-s", "need": "The bench lacks the $1.25 a day headcount that Target 1.1 names. A series at the original 2011 PPP line, back to 1981 or 1990, would allow a like-for-like 2015 baseline and a true test of the 2030 goal.", "shelf examples": ["SH.DYN.MORT", "SI.POV.DDAY", "SP.POP.TOTL"]}

{"tool": {"name": "national-poverty-line-metadata", "about": "Screens a series for large changes between consecutive survey years per country, to flag candidate definitional breaks (such as poverty-line revisions) for follow-up. The World Bank data supply no line metadata, so flags are candidates only.", "params": {"series": "Series code to screen, which must also appear in series_params", "jump_threshold": "Smallest absolute change between consecutive observed years to flag, in the series unit; default 5.0", "country": "Optional country code to restrict the screen to one country"}, "code": "def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    gap = params.get('jump_threshold', 5.0)
    country = params.get('country')
    s = data[code]
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    flagged = []
    counted = 0
    obs_total = 0
    for unit in s:
        series = s[unit]
        if unit not in regions:
            continue
        if country is not None and unit != country:
            continue
        years = sorted(series.keys())
        if len(years) == 0:
            continue
        counted += 1
        obs_total += len(years)
        for i in range(1, len(years)):
            a = series[years[i-1]]
            b = series[years[i]]
            d = b - a
            if abs(d) >= gap:
                flagged.append((abs(d), unit, years[i-1], years[i], d))
    flagged.sort(reverse=True)
    top = flagged[:5]
    facts = {'countries_with_data': counted, 'observations': obs_total, 'jumps_flagged': len(flagged), 'threshold': gap}
    if top:
        t = top[0]
        facts['largest_jump_country'] = names.get(t[1], t[1])
        facts['largest_jump_from_year'] = t[2]
        facts['largest_jump_to_year'] = t[3]
        facts['largest_jump_value'] = round(t[4], 2)
    parts = []
    for t in top:
        parts.append(names.get(t[1], t[1]) + ' ' + str(t[2]) + ' to ' + str(t[3]) + ': ' + str(round(t[4], 2)))
    summary = 'Between consecutive survey years, ' + str(len(flagged)) + ' changes of at least ' + str(gap) + ' were found across ' + str(counted) + ' countries (' + str(obs_total) + ' observations). The data carry no poverty-line metadata, so a jump marks a candidate definitional revision to check against national sources, not a confirmed one. '
    if parts:
        summary += 'Largest: ' + '; '.join(parts) + '.'

answer.comments:
Most figures match their facts, but several do not.

S1: '81 per cent' is derived, not a fact (34.89/19.31 is about 80.7 per cent; acceptable only if flagged, as it is). 'US$59,999.9987 in 2000' is a fact but is a trivial series. The text states South Asia 2025 (11.3173%) on '60 reporting countries', but the 60 is the 2025 count, which is fine. Numbers 2016 vs 2015 for MENAAP are correct.

S2: The heading 'Aid has grown in every region reported' is unsupported for North America, whose series is only 2000 and 2004. Say 'in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series'. Aid for poverty reduction is not answered; state this plainly up front.

S3: The 'largest proportional rise' claim needs all regional ratios computed; Sub-Saharan Africa rose about 39 per cent, so it holds, but show it. The proposal on constant prices follows from the findings.

S5: The final 'Proposals' section is a stub; either list the proposals or cut it. The Sub-Saharan Africa health paragraph is clear.

answer.code:
def tool(data, params):
    codes = params['series_codes'] if 'series_codes' in params else []
    start = params.get('start_year', 2000)
    facts = {}
    lines = []
    for code in codes:
        units = data[code] if code in data else {}
        best = None
        for unit in units:
            ser = units[unit]
            ys = [int(y) for y in ser if int(y) >= start and ser[y] is not None]
            if not ys:
                continue
            ly = max(ys)
            vals = [ser[y] for y in ser if int(y) == ly and ser[y] is not None]
            if best is None or ly > best[0]:
                best = (ly, unit, len(ys), vals[0] if vals else None, ys)
        if best is None:
            facts[code + '_status'] = 'no data'
            lines.append(code + ': no data since ' + str(start) + '.')
            continue
        ly, unit, n, v, ys = best
        ser = units[unit]
        early = min(ys)
        ev = [ser[y] for y in ser if int(y) == early][0]
        vs = [ser[y] for y in ser if int(y) >= start and ser[y] is not None]
        facts[code + '_latest'] = v
        facts[code + '_latest_year'] = ly
        facts[code + '_unit'] = unit
        facts[code + '_first_year'] = early
        facts[code + '_first'] = ev
        facts[code + '_mean'] = round(statistics.mean(vs), 4)
        facts[code + '_n_obs'] = n
        lines.append(code + ': ' + str(v) + ' (' + unit + ') in ' + str(ly) + '; ' + str(ev) + ' in ' + str(early) + '; ' + str(n) + ' observations from ' + str(start) + '.')
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': ' '.join(lines) + ' Missing years are not interpolated.'}

Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built, and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced. The World Development Indicators offer one series that bears directly on exposure: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. The series counts displacement events, not distinct people, so one person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It also says nothing about income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Losses in money, lives or livelihoods are not measured by it. The question of how many people were affected, and what losses followed, can therefore be answered only in part, through displacement.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19188817 cases in 2015 and reached 26393278 cases in 2023. The increase over the period is substantial, but the two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because disaster displacement varies sharply from year to year with the severity of storms, floods and other events. A further caution applies to the comparison: the number of reporting countries changed over the period, as the next section shows.

### Regional contrasts

The regional picture diverges more than the global total suggests. East Asia and Pacific recorded 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023, and remains the largest regional source of new displacement in both years. South Asia moved in the opposite direction, from 6877900 cases in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of this size is more likely to reflect the particular events of the two years than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1108287 cases in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 cases in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because the figure for 2015 is not given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1212730 cases in 2015 to 2481660 in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These regional movements matter for the target because the regions where displacement has grown most quickly include some with large populations living in poverty. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the ones displaced, only that exposure to displacing events grew most where the regional counts rose most.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed greatly. It was 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009, and stood at 73 in 2010, 62 in 2011 and 79 in 2012. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014, and reached 112 in 2015. Later figures were 116 in 2016, 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018, 136 in 2019, 142 in 2020, 133 in 2021, 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

The consequence is that part of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may be a product of wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are therefore not a like-for-like comparison. Earlier years are weaker still, and no trend should be drawn from the period before 2013.

### Concentration of displacement is increasing

Inequality among countries in displacement, weighted by population, has widened. The Gini coefficient was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893 over the same years, and the coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: displacement is more concentrated in a smaller number of countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of the Theil index that lies between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015, then, most of the inequality came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share arises from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages therefore hide more than they once did, and a response designed by region would miss a growing part of the concentration. The comparison should be read with the caution already given, as the sample grew from 112 to 145 countries.

Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate is available for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

Coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, measured as a percentage of that quintile, rests on household surveys. Survey timing therefore sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000 two countries reported, and in 2002 three. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013. The results do not say why the count fell, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count fell: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only one country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was measured for three years. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality falls

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a marked change. In 2015, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index. By 2018 the between-region share was 28.8 per cent, and by 2021 it was 21.4 per cent. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. In 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region.

The size of the change suggests that the composition of the sample, and not only government policy, may drive the result. The data given here do not allow that explanation to be tested.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only one country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. carried.comments: S1: Numbers match their facts, but gini 0.570/0.678 and Theil 0.723/0.893 are rounded from 0.5701/0.6783 and 0.7232/0.8935; write them as the results give them. Large counts lack thousands separators; the unit (cases) is missing in places. S3: 'Inequality ... has widened' and 'more concentrated' overreach given the coverage rise (112 to 145). The claim that regions with rising displacement 'include some with large populations living in poverty' has no cited poverty result; cut it or source it. 'Remains the largest regional source in both years' is unsupported for 2015 and 2023 without a ranking, though it follows from the figures. The proposal on household poverty data is not grounded in a finding. S2: the question's losses are unanswered beyond a caveat; state clearly what is unanswered. S5: the 'Displacement as the measure' heading is not a finding; the 2008 to 2012 coverage list is too long, so summarise it. 'Proposals follow' is a placeholder heading.

Numbers check against the facts: counts, Gini, Theil, CV and shares all match (74.1, 28.8, 21.4 per cent round 0.7408, 0.2878, 0.2137). Problems: (1) The text says a fall from 41 in 2012 to 24 in 2013 and that 2022 and 2023 are lower than 2018, which is fine, but 'in 2000 two countries' and 'three' are written as words while facts are integers; keep digits and give units consistently (countries). answer.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, and the facts available here contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. What can be said comes from the classification of trends, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Population shares are given to one decimal place and are rounded from finer values.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Divergence appears in a small group

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 relates each country's change in headcount to its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The sign is positive, which does not indicate catching up; the facts do not give the direction of the underlying changes, so whether the pattern reflects larger increases or smaller falls cannot be told.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence points to divergence among these 25 countries, but the group is small and may not represent all countries.

### Proposals

Each proposal below follows from a finding above.

proposals: Because only 52 countries reported a national-line headcount for 2022 and 13 for 2025, national statistical offices and their funders should prioritise completing and publishing recent household survey estimates, so that progress after 2015 can be assessed.

Because neither the national-line nor the multidimensional series has an aggregate, the custodians should publish a documented aggregate, or state why none is possible, so that a worldwide change can be read.

Because the rank link between national and international lines is weaker for change (Spearman 0.3763) than for level (0.6486), reports should present both measures side by side and flag any revision to a national line.

Because 34 of 94 assessed countries are regressing and the 25-country test points to divergence, national plans should target the countries with high starting headcounts first and monitor them closely.
answer.gaps: The data give no country-level headcount values or changes, so the direction and size of change cannot be stated, and there is no global or regional aggregate for either series. Coverage falls steeply after 2021. Trend classes cover 94 countries, the line comparison 21 and the convergence test 25, so these may not represent all countries. Changes in national definitions are not recorded, and the evidence does not show how much reporting lag explains the thin recent years. Target 1.2 can be read as a halving of each country's own headcount or of a global proportion; the data do not settle which.

answer.text:
Target 1.4 asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated. They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered, and urban populations are absent from the rural series. Rural coverage is therefore only a proxy: the findings show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the present pace holds, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, a far lower level than the other regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is available among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%. Its rate of 0.07583 is still classed as marginal progress, and the expected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, listed below.

No 2030 projection for rural sanitation is available among the results. The sanitation trend classes cover the whole population, not rural populations. Quality, affordability and reliability of services are not covered, and the 100% target can be read as universal basic access or as a higher service standard.

answer.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. The trend tool gives an expected world value of 8.365 per cent in 2030. It rates progress as marginal, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions are classed differently. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. The data do not say why either region moved as it did.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. The count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 should be made with that caution.

carried.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, and the facts available here contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. What can be said comes from the classification of trends, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Population shares are given to one decimal place and are rounded from finer values.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Divergence appears in a small group

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 relates each country's change in headcount to its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The sign is positive, which does not indicate catching up; the facts do not give the direction of the underlying changes, so whether the pattern reflects larger increases or smaller falls cannot be told.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence points to divergence among these 25 countries, but the group is small and may not represent all countries.

### Proposals

Each proposal below follows from a finding above.

proposals: Because only 52 countries reported a national-line headcount for 2022 and 13 for 2025, national statistical offices and their funders should prioritise completing and publishing recent household survey estimates, so that progress after 2015 can be assessed.

Because neither the national-line nor the multidimensional series has an aggregate, the custodians should publish a documented aggregate, or state why none is possible, so that a worldwide change can be read.

Because the rank link between national and international lines is weaker for change (Spearman 0.3763) than for level (0.6486), reports should present both measures side by side and flag any revision to a national line.

Because 34 of 94 assessed countries are regressing and the 25-country test points to divergence, national plans should target the countries with high starting headcounts first and monitor them closely.

Coverage falls steeply after 2021. Trend classes cover 94 countries, the line comparison 21 and the convergence test 25, so these may not represent all countries. Changes in national definitions are not recorded, and the evidence does not show how much reporting lag explains the thin recent years. Target 1.2 can be read as a halving of each country's own headcount or of a global proportion; the data do not settle which.
