carried.text:
Target 1.4 asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated. They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered, and urban populations are absent from the rural series. Rural coverage is therefore only a proxy: the findings show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the present pace holds, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, a far lower level than the other regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is available among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%. Its rate of 0.07583 is still classed as marginal progress, and the expected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, listed below.

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, and the facts available here contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. What can be said comes from the classification of trends, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Population shares are given to one decimal place and are rounded from finer values.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Divergence appears in a small group

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 relates each country's change in headcount to its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The sign is positive, which does not indicate catching up; the facts do not give the direction of the underlying changes, so whether the pattern reflects larger increases or smaller falls cannot be told.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence points to divergence among these 25 countries, but the group is small and may not represent all countries.

### Proposals

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Extreme poverty falls but misses zero", "question": "What share of people lived below the international poverty line in 2015 and in the latest year?", "targets": [{"target": "1.1", "text": "By 2030, eradicate extreme poverty for all people everywhere, currently measured as people living on less than $1.25 a day"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. The trend tool gives an expected world value of 8.365 per cent in 2030. It rates progress as marginal, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions are classed differently. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. The data do not say why either region moved as it did.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. The count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015. answer.comments:
Most figures match their facts: 13.4 and 10.1 per cent, 8.365, 0.376, the regional values, the 105-country shares (0.4555 as 45.55 per cent) and the break means. Two points need correction.

S1: the text gives 'a ratio of -0.481' and similar figures without noting that these ratios are the tool's measure of progress against the required pace. Also, 'the $3.00 a day in 2021 prices' line, the '2001 to 2013' period and 'nine years of data' are not facts of any cited result. Derive or remove them, or cite their source. The 'four years' window for South Asia is inferred from 2020 to 2024, which is five annual points, so correct it.

S3: the claim that the 2024 regional values rest on far fewer reporting countries is sound, but 'Each period is slower than the one before' skips the 2019 to 2020 gap; say so. The proposal to study 24 regression countries follows from the findings. The proposal to fund surveys should note that no cause is established for falling coverage.

Rural coverage is therefore only a proxy: the findings show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the present pace holds, far below the target.

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. ### Education shares fell in most regions

The question asked of this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. The data answer the first part only in terms of budget shares. They do not answer the second part, because the aid series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid.

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but most regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares also differ. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. End years differ by region, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they show the size of the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. That is a rise of about 81 per cent, calculated by the cooperative from these two figures and not itself a reported fact. Sub-Saharan Africa rose by a smaller proportion on the same basis, so the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series; its aid is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, both in current dollars, and is no meaningful comparator.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

### Education shares fell in most regions

The question asked of this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. The data answer the first part only in terms of budget shares. They do not answer the second part, because the aid series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid.

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but most regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares also differ. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. End years differ by region, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they show the size of the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. That is a rise of about 81 per cent, calculated by the cooperative from these two figures and not itself a reported fact. Sub-Saharan Africa rose by a smaller proportion on the same basis, so the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series; its aid is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, both in current dollars, and is no meaningful comparator.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

### Proposals

The proposals follow from the findings above. They are also listed in the proposals field.

proposals: Statistical agencies should report education and health spending per child and per person in constant prices alongside budget shares, so that shares can be read against need.
Donors should tag aid by poverty-reduction purpose in the series reported to the World Bank, so that aid for poverty reduction can be separated from other aid.

Governments and the World Bank should report the benefit incidence of social protection to the poorest fifth every year, and extend regional aggregates to East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan for health spending.
Aid series should be published in constant prices, so that real growth can be told from price effects.
carried.gaps: The data do not separate aid for poverty reduction from other aid, give no spending per child or per person, and carry no measure of need. Aid regional series end in 2021 and North America has no 2015 to 2021 series. Regional health series end as early as 2019, and two regions have no health aggregate. Social protection incidence has no aggregates and thin, erratic coverage. Nothing here measures whether spending reaches the poorest households, or whether policy frameworks are gender-sensitive.

carried.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several points need correcting. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity: the text calls 0.07583 a rate and 'marginal'; the fact confirms marginal, but the 2030 value of 55.3497% is stated as 'if the present pace holds' without the unit of the rate. State the unit or cut it. (2) 'North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target' is fine for water, but North America's 2030 value is 101.27%, above 100%; note this is a projection artefact. (3) The sanitation 'on track' share 46.64% and the 'regression' 13.36% are given, but the sentence about 'average improvement' is unsupported; cut it. (4) The 'Proposals' heading ends with 'listed below' and no list; remove or merge. (5) Proposal 1 omits sanitation, where Sub-Saharan Africa is furthest behind (27.0945%). (6) The 'poor' question is answered only through proxy; say plainly that the answer is largely negative. (7) The claim 'Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster' needs the sign of beta stated.

Most figures match their facts: 13.4 and 10.1 per cent, 8.365, 0.376, the regional values, the 105-country shares (0.4555 as 45.55 per cent) and the break means. Two points need correction.

S1: the text gives 'a ratio of -0.481' and similar figures without noting that these ratios are the tool's measure of progress against the required pace. Also, 'the $3.00 a day in 2021 prices' line, the '2001 to 2013' period and 'nine years of data' are not facts of any cited result. Derive or remove them, or cite their source. The 'four years' window for South Asia is inferred from 2020 to 2024, which is five annual points, so correct it.

S3: the claim that the 2024 regional values rest on far fewer reporting countries is sound, but 'Each period is slower than the one before' skips the 2019 to 2020 gap; say so. The proposal to study 24 regression countries follows from the findings. The proposal to fund surveys should note that no cause is established for falling coverage.

Numbers: the regression population share is given as 26.0%, but the fact is 0.2596, so write 26.0% only if rounded (0.2596 rounds to 26.0%, acceptable). The moderate-progress share 3.8% (0.0376) and marginal 4.4% (0.0436) round correctly. Check the section heading 'Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern': the section claims similarity without support, and 'better populated in most middle years' is not stated as a fact. The question asks how headcounts changed; the text admits it cannot say, which is honest, but the answer is therefore thin. The convergence beta of 0.025885 is read as positive divergence, yet the dependent variable's direction is unknown; soften 'evidence points to divergence'. Proposal 4 (target high-headcount countries first) goes beyond the findings; tie it to the data or cut it. The proposals section opening line is filler; cut it. Rounding note on population shares is misplaced.

Numbers match their facts, but several statements go beyond the results. (1) 'Sub-Saharan Africa rate of 0.07583' is given without a unit or meaning; state it or cut it. (2) 'North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target' omits the Sub-Saharan trend rate caveat; fine, but Europe & Central Asia is also on track for electricity, which is not mentioned. (3) The proposal to 'investigate the 39 countries' is a whole-population sanitation finding, not rural, and the 13.36% is of assessed population; keep the wording but do not tie it to rural gaps. (4) The 'Proposals' section ends with 'listed below' but no list appears in the text; add the three proposals. (5) The opening says urban populations are absent, yet the first proposal ranks water and electricity above sanitation, where Sub-Saharan Africa is weakest (27.0945%); add sanitation. (6) The unsupported claim that deprivation is 'concentrated' in rural areas has no cited fact; cut or qualify it. (7) The section never states that the poor's access is unmeasured in its conclusion.

answer.about: Summarises the latest available value of one series per country within a year window: coverage, median, mean, extremes and regional medians. Used as a national baseline and coverage check while no wealth-quintile access series exists in the indicators; it makes plain that national figures are no substitute for quintile data.

params.name: series
params.meaning: World Development Indicators series code to summarise

params.name: start_year
params.meaning: First year of the window, inclusive

params.name: end_year
params.meaning: Last year of the window, inclusive

cases.expect: facts show countries_with_data well below countries_total (poverty surveys are sparse), a median poverty headcount in per cent of population, and regional medians; summary notes that the series is national and latest years differ.

facts show near-full coverage, a median under-five mortality per 1,000 live births, lowest and highest countries named with years, and regional medians; summary repeats the caveat that no quintile split exists.

"c02-5.r3: countries 2023": 145}, "previous version": {"text": "### Displacement as the measure of disaster exposure

Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built, and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced. The World Development Indicators offer one series that bears directly on exposure: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. The series counts displacement events, not distinct people, so one person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It also says nothing about income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Losses in money, lives or livelihoods are not measured by it. The question of how many people were affected, and what losses followed, can therefore be answered only in part, through displacement.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19188817 cases in 2015 and reached 26393278 cases in 2023. The increase over the period is substantial, but the two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because disaster displacement varies sharply from year to year with the severity of storms, floods and other events. A further caution applies to the comparison: the number of reporting countries changed over the period, as the next section shows.

### Regional contrasts

The regional picture diverges more than the global total suggests. East Asia and Pacific recorded 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023, and remains the largest regional source of new displacement in both years. South Asia moved in the opposite direction, from 6877900 cases in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of this size is more likely to reflect the particular events of the two years than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1108287 cases in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 cases in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because the figure for 2015 is not given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1212730 cases in 2015 to 2481660 in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These regional movements matter for the target because the regions where displacement has grown most quickly include some with large populations living in poverty. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the ones displaced, only that exposure to displacing events grew most where the regional counts rose most.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed greatly. It was 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009, and stood at 73 in 2010, 62 in 2011 and 79 in 2012. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014, and reached 112 in 2015. Later figures were 116 in 2016, 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018, 136 in 2019, 142 in 2020, 133 in 2021, 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

The consequence is that part of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may be a product of wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are therefore not a like-for-like comparison. Earlier years are weaker still, and no trend should be drawn from the period before 2013.

### Concentration of displacement is increasing

Inequality among countries in displacement, weighted by population, has widened. The Gini coefficient was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893 over the same years, and the coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: displacement is more concentrated in a smaller number of countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of the Theil index that lies between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015, then, most of the inequality came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share arises from differences among countries within regions. Regional averages therefore hide more than they once did, and a response designed by region would miss a growing part of the concentration. The comparison should be read with the caution already given, as the sample grew from 112 to 145 countries.

### Proposals follow

answer.text:
### Disaster displacement rose to 26,393,278 cases in 2023

Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built, and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced. The World Development Indicators carry one series that bears directly on exposure: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. The series counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. It also records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. The part of the question concerning losses therefore cannot be answered with this series; only the number of displacement cases can be reported.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because disaster displacement depends heavily on the severity of the storms, floods and other events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023. These are the highest regional figures in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where displacing events grew, not who was displaced. The data used here do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. Between 2008 and 2012 it ranged from 60 countries (2009) to 80 countries (2008), too few and too unstable to support a trend. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015 most of the unevenness came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share came from differences among countries within regions. A response designed only by region would therefore miss a growing part of the unevenness.

### Proposals

The findings support the proposals below.

c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Statistical offices and international agencies should publish a harmonised panel of the countries reporting throughout the period, so that changes in displacement can be separated from changes in reporting.
Countries should report disaster displacement alongside economic loss and mortality in a common format, so that the losses that follow displacement can be measured.
Where displacement records exist, they should be linked to household survey data on income, so that the number of poor people displaced can be estimated.
Disaster-resilience planning should be set at national level as well as regional level, since a growing share of the spread in displacement lies among countries within regions.
answer.gaps: The series counts displacement cases, not distinct people, and gives no information on income, so the number of poor people affected is not known. No data on monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods were used, so the losses that followed are not measured. The rise in reporting countries from 112 in 2015 to 145 in 2023 limits like-for-like comparison, and the two end years may not represent the years between them.

The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3 countries. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 countries in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 countries in 2013. The results do not say why the count fell, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count fell: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage (percentage of the poorest quintile) among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These years are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and the latest year with a reasonably large sample. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage; this is a hypothesis that the available results cannot test. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality falls

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a marked change. In 2015, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index. By 2018 the between-region share was 28.8 per cent, and by 2021 it was 21.4 per cent. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. In 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region. The change in sample composition between years makes it uncertain how much of this shift is real.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only 1 country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding for this section concerns the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse and irregular, and the count of reporting countries was lower in 2022, at 17, than in 2018, at 47.

The World Development Indicators carry one series that bears directly on exposure: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. The series counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. It also records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. The part of the question concerning losses therefore cannot be answered with this series; only the number of displacement cases can be reported.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because disaster displacement depends heavily on the severity of the storms, floods and other events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023. These are the highest regional figures in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where displacing events grew, not who was displaced. The data used here do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. Between 2008 and 2012 it ranged from 60 countries (2009) to 80 countries (2008), too few and too unstable to support a trend. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.570 in 2015 and 0.678 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015 most of the unevenness came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share came from differences among countries within regions. A response designed only by region would therefore miss a growing part of the unevenness.

### Proposals

The findings support the proposals below.

proposals: Statistical offices and international agencies should publish a harmonised panel of the countries reporting throughout the period, so that changes in displacement can be separated from changes in reporting.
Countries should report disaster displacement alongside economic loss and mortality in a common format, so that the losses that follow displacement can be measured.
Where displacement records exist, they should be linked to household survey data on income, so that the number of poor people displaced can be estimated.
Disaster-resilience planning should be set at national level as well as regional level, since a growing share of the spread in displacement lies among countries within regions.
carried.gaps: The series counts displacement cases, not distinct people, and gives no information on income, so the number of poor people affected is not known. No data on monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods were used, so the losses that followed are not measured. The rise in reporting countries from 112 in 2015 to 145 in 2023 limits like-for-like comparison, and the two end years may not represent the years between them.

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Resources and pro-poor spending are uneven", "question": "How much do governments spend on essential services, and how much aid supports poverty reduction?", "targets": [{"target": "1.a", "text": "Ensure significant mobilization of resources from a variety of sources, including through enhanced development cooperation, in order to provide adequate and predictable means for developing countries, in particular least developed countries, to implement programmes and policies to end poverty in all"}, {"target": "1.b", "text": "Create sound policy frameworks at the national, regional and international levels, based on pro-poor and gender-sensitive development strategies, to support accelerated investment in poverty eradication actions"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "### Education shares fell in most regions

The question asked of this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. The data answer the first part only in terms of budget shares. They do not answer the second part, because the aid series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid.

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but most regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares also differ. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. End years differ by region, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they show the size of the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. That is a rise of about 81 per cent, calculated by the cooperative from these two figures and not itself a reported fact. Sub-Saharan Africa rose by a smaller proportion on the same basis, so the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series; its aid is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, both in current dollars, and is no meaningful comparator.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

answer.comments: S1: Most figures match their facts. The text gives 'about 81 per cent' for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rise; it is flagged as derived, which is acceptable, and it is correct (about 80.7). The claim that Sub-Saharan Africa rose by less is also derived and not stated with a figure; give it (about 39 per cent). The 2000 and 2004 North America aid figures are not in the 2015 to 2021 comparison and add little; cut or explain. The 60 countries for 2025 is a fact, but South Asia is a regional figure, so say the count refers to the series and not to South Asia alone. S2: the aid question is answered only by saying the data cannot answer it; the opening sentence on spending as 'essential services' covers education and health only, so name that limit. S3: the proposals are listed but not given in the text; the closing section only points to them. State them there. 'Aid rose in every region' is true for the listed regions but North America is excluded; make the heading say so. S5: the proposals heading is empty; fill it.

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Resources and pro-poor spending are uneven", "question": "How much do governments spend on essential services, and how much aid supports poverty reduction?", "targets": [{"target": "1.a", "text": "Ensure significant mobilization of resources from a variety of sources, including through enhanced development cooperation, in order to provide adequate and predictable means for developing countries, in particular least developed countries, to implement programmes and policies to end poverty in all"}, {"target": "1.b", "text": "Create sound policy frameworks at the national, regional and international levels, based on pro-poor and gender-sensitive development strategies, to support accelerated investment in poverty eradication actions"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "### Education shares fell in most regions

The question asked of this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. The data answer the first part only in terms of budget shares. They do not answer the second part, because the aid series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid.

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but most regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares also differ. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. End years differ by region, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they show the size of the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. That is a rise of about 81 per cent, calculated by the cooperative from these two figures and not itself a reported fact. Sub-Saharan Africa rose by a smaller proportion on the same basis, so the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series; its aid is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, both in current dollars, and is no meaningful comparator.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3 countries. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 countries in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 countries in 2013. The results do not say why the count fell, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count fell: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage (percentage of the poorest quintile) among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These years are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and the latest year with a reasonably large sample. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage; this is a hypothesis that the available results cannot test. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a marked change. In 2015, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index. By 2018 the between-region share was 28.8 per cent, and by 2021 it was 21.4 per cent. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. In 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region. The change in sample composition between years makes it uncertain how much of this shift is real.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only 1 country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world.

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The part of the question concerning losses therefore cannot be answered with this series; only the number of displacement cases can be reported.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. Between 2008 and 2012 it ranged from 60 countries (2009) to 80 countries (2008), too few and too unstable to support a trend. A response designed only by region would therefore miss a growing part of the unevenness.

answer.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), was reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it. The facts available contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. The answer to the question of change rests on the trend classification, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional coverage follows a comparable course

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate, and both series lose coverage towards the present. Only coverage is compared here; the facts give no values for this indicator.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion widened in a small group

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 relates each country's change in headcount to its starting level. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. A negative coefficient would indicate that higher starters fell faster; this one is positive, so the test gives no sign of catching up. The facts do not state how the change was measured or its direction, so the sign cannot be read as proof of rising or falling poverty.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. This is consistent with divergence, but the group is small and may not represent all countries.

Fund survey programmes and faster release so that the 2023 to 2025 counts (40, 31 and 13 countries) approach the 72 reporting in 2021, since the latest years are the least complete.
Report national-line and $3.00-a-day headcounts side by side, because the rank correlation of changes (0.3763) is too weak for either to stand in for the other.
Repeat the convergence test when more countries report, since the 25-country result on a positive beta and a wider coefficient of variation cannot be generalised.

answer.text:
Target 1.4 asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and cover rural populations. They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered, and the rural series say nothing about urban populations. Rural coverage is therefore only a proxy for the poor. The plain answer to the question of whether the poor are shown to be reached is largely negative: the data show where service gaps lie between regions, but they cannot show who within a region is left out. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. North America's expected 2030 value is 101.2664%, which exceeds 100% only because the projection extends a linear trend and cannot be read as real coverage. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the 2015 to 2024 trend continues, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, by far the lowest level among the regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population, and is not a rural finding. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the assessed population.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024. The beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The negative sign means that countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024, so the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale yet still classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 55.3497% on the present trend. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal progress, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to the priorities below.
