answer.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030, and its text refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a different, revised line from the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which is the goal the trend tool uses.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. The trend tool gives an expected world value of 8.365 per cent in 2030. It rates progress as marginal, with significant acceleration needed. Its ratio is 0.376, which is the tool's measure of progress achieved set against the pace the target requires; a ratio of 1 or more would mean on track. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification, set out in the figure for result c02-1.r3, separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of five annual points, 2020 to 2024, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions whose series begin in 2015.

Two regions are classed differently. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent. Its negative ratio of -0.481 means movement away from the target, and the tool classes it as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. The data do not say why either region moved as it did.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r5, finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each reported segment is slower than the one before. The segments do not cover 2019 and 2020, so the pace in those years is not described here.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. The count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 should be made with that caution. The data give no cause for the fall in reporting.

### Proposals

The proposals follow from these findings and are listed below.

carried.text:
Target 1.4 asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and cover rural populations. They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered, and the rural series say nothing about urban populations. Rural coverage is therefore only a proxy for the poor. The plain answer to the question of whether the poor are shown to be reached is largely negative: the data show where service gaps lie between regions, but they cannot show who within a region is left out. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. North America's expected 2030 value is 101.2664%, which exceeds 100% only because the projection extends a linear trend and cannot be read as real coverage. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the 2015 to 2024 trend continues, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, by far the lowest level among the regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population, and is not a rural finding. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the assessed population.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024. The beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The negative sign means that countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024, so the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale yet still classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 55.3497% on the present trend. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal progress, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to the priorities below.

carried.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), was reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it. The facts available contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. The answer to the question of change rests on the trend classification, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional coverage follows a comparable course

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate, and both series lose coverage towards the present. Only coverage is compared here; the facts give no values for this indicator.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion widened in a small group

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 relates each country's change in headcount to its starting level. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. A negative coefficient would indicate that higher starters fell faster; this one is positive, so the test gives no sign of catching up. The facts do not state how the change was measured or its direction, so the sign cannot be read as proof of rising or falling poverty.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. This is consistent with divergence, but the group is small and may not represent all countries.

carried.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030, and its text refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a different, revised line from the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which is the goal the trend tool uses.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. The trend tool gives an expected world value of 8.365 per cent in 2030. It rates progress as marginal, with significant acceleration needed. Its ratio is 0.376, which is the tool's measure of progress achieved set against the pace the target requires; a ratio of 1 or more would mean on track. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification, set out in the figure for result c02-1.r3, separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of five annual points, 2020 to 2024, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions whose series begin in 2015.

Two regions are classed differently. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent. Its negative ratio of -0.481 means movement away from the target, and the tool classes it as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. The data do not say why either region moved as it did.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r5, finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each reported segment is slower than the one before. The segments do not cover 2019 and 2020, so the pace in those years is not described here.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. The count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 should be made with that caution. The data give no cause for the fall in reporting.

### Proposals

The proposals follow from these findings and are listed below.

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Extreme poverty falls but misses zero", "question": "What share of people lived below the international poverty line in 2015 and in the latest year?", "targets": [{"target": "1.1", "text": "By 2030, eradicate extreme poverty for all people everywhere, currently measured as people living on less than $1.25 a day"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030, and its text refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a different, revised line from the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which is the goal the trend tool uses.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. The trend tool gives an expected world value of 8.365 per cent in 2030. It rates progress as marginal, with significant acceleration needed. Its ratio is 0.376, which is the tool's measure of progress achieved set against the pace the target requires; a ratio of 1 or more would mean on track. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification, set out in the figure for result c02-1.r3, separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of five annual points, 2020 to 2024, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions whose series begin in 2015.

Two regions are classed differently. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent. Its negative ratio of -0.481 means movement away from the target, and the tool classes it as regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. The data do not say why either region moved as it did.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r5, finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each reported segment is slower than the one before. The segments do not cover 2019 and 2020, so the pace in those years is not described here.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. The count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 should be made with that caution. The data give no cause for the fall in reporting.

### Proposals

The plain answer to the question of whether the poor are shown to be reached is largely negative: the data show where service gaps lie between regions, but they cannot show who within a region is left out. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. North America's expected 2030 value is 101.2664%, which exceeds 100% only because the projection extends a linear trend and cannot be read as real coverage. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the 2015 to 2024 trend continues, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, by far the lowest level among the regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population, and is not a rural finding. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the assessed population.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024. The beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The negative sign means that countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024, so the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale yet still classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 55.3497% on the present trend. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal progress, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), was reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. The data do not show how much of this is reporting lag and how much is a lack of surveys.

The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it. The facts available contain no country-level values or changes in the headcount. How the headcount changed in absolute terms, and in which direction in each country, therefore cannot be stated. The answer to the question of change rests on the trend classification, the comparison with the international line and the convergence test below.

### Multidimensional coverage follows a comparable course

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate, and both series lose coverage towards the present. Only coverage is compared here; the facts give no values for this indicator.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The facts do not state how the change was measured or its direction, so the sign cannot be read as proof of rising or falling poverty.

answer.about: Summarises the latest observation per country within a year window for one World Bank series: coverage, median, mean, extremes with years, and regional medians. Built to be pointed at disaster-loss or death series once available, and meanwhile usable on any shelf series.

params.name: series
params.meaning: Code of the series to summarise; must be listed in series_params.

params.name: start_year
params.meaning: First year of the window (default 2000).

params.name: end_year
params.meaning: Last year of the window (default 2022).

cases.expect: Facts show a large country count (well over 150), a median under-five mortality in deaths per 1,000 live births of roughly 15 to 20, a highest value above 70 for a West African country, a lowest value below 5, and regional medians; summary names extremes with years.

Fewer countries than for mortality because of sparse survey coverage; coverage_pct clearly below 100; median poverty rate at the international line in per cent of population is low single digits to around ten; highest values in sub-Saharan Africa; summary notes that missing countries are excluded.

The plain answer to the question of whether the poor are shown to be reached is largely negative: the data show where service gaps lie between regions, but they cannot show who within a region is left out. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668% in 2024. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. North America's expected 2030 value is 101.2664%, which exceeds 100% only because the projection extends a linear trend and cannot be read as real coverage. Sub-Saharan Africa is classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914% if the 2015 to 2024 trend continues, far below the target.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia rose from 50.4934% to 79.8838% and East Asia & Pacific from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, by far the lowest level among the regions shown for 2024. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 rural sanitation value is among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged from levels alone.

The sanitation trend to target covers the whole population, not only the rural population, and is not a rural finding. It classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. The regressing countries hold 13.36% of the assessed population.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries from 2015 to 2024. The beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The negative sign means that countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024, so the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access narrows gaps but leaves Sub-Saharan Africa far behind

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale yet still classed as marginal progress, with an expected 2030 value of 55.3497% on the present trend. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is also classed as marginal progress, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

answer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several claims do not follow. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity is called 'the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale': meaningless; its 17.2-point gain exceeds every other region's, so say 'largest regional gain'. South Asia's expected 2030 electricity value (114.3542%) is omitted, though it is on track. (2) Rural sanitation: the text says no projection exists, true for the cited facts, but 'South Asia and Europe & Central Asia on track' for electricity and water are unmentioned; Europe & Central Asia is on track in electricity. (3) Sub-Saharan Africa water 'far below the target' is fine, but sanitation levels alone cannot show 'pace'; say so plainly. (4) The final heading 'Proposals follow from the gaps' ends on one line, and the proposals are not stated in the text; add them or cut the heading. (5) Cut 'fastest ... scale'; give the electricity world trend its expected 2030 value, 90.9205%. (6) Say rural sanitation Latin America and Middle East regions also lag.

in any year": 193}, "previous version": {"text": "### Education shares fell in most regions

The question asked of this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. The data answer the first part only in terms of budget shares. They do not answer the second part, because the aid series does not separate aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid.

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but most regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares also differ. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. End years differ by region, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical. The South Asian endpoint of 2025 rests on only 60 reporting countries, a thin base. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. These data give no measure of need, so they show the size of the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. That is a rise of about 81 per cent, calculated by the cooperative from these two figures and not itself a reported fact. Sub-Saharan Africa rose by a smaller proportion on the same basis, so the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series; its aid is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, both in current dollars, and is no meaningful comparator.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

answer.text:
### Education shares fell in most regions

The question put to this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. Essential services are covered here by two budget shares only, education and health. No series available to the bench separates aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid, so no figure for pro-poor aid exists in these data.

Government expenditure on education, as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but five of the seven regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 16.9629% in 2015 to 15.3772% in 2024, a large drop from the highest starting share. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022, and Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024.

End years differ from 2022 to 2025, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical and comparisons between regions are indicative only. The count of 60 countries reporting in 2025 belongs to the education series as a whole, not to South Asia alone; it shows that the most recent endpoints rest on a thin base. A budget share is not an amount per child and does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. The data give no measure of need, so they show the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. The rise for that region is about 81 per cent and for Sub-Saharan Africa about 39 per cent; both percentages are calculated by the cooperative from the figures given and are not reported facts. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region therefore had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series and is left out of this comparison; its only recorded values are trivial, US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

### Proposals

First, aid reporting should flag the share of aid directed to poverty reduction, so that Target 1.a can be assessed. Second, aid should be published in constant prices alongside current dollars. Third, education and health spending should be reported per child and per person as well as by budget share. Fourth, countries should report the benefit incidence of social protection to the poorest fifth every year, so that a trend can be built.

carried.comments: Numbers match their facts, but some statements do not follow the results. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity: 'fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale' is unclear and unsupported; South Asia gained 18.4 points against 17.2, so drop or restate. (2) South Asia water is called 'on track or met' while 2024 is 95.2211% and the 2030 value 100.176% is a linear artefact; say so. (3) Sanitation 'by far the lowest' is fine, but the first proposal says 'lowest of any region' while only some regions are shown; name all regions or cite the full set. (4) Electricity: Latin America & Caribbean 'marginal progress' is correct for the 2030 trend, but the world water trend should be stated as 'marginal progress' consistently. (5) The 'Proposals follow from the gaps' section ends with one stub sentence and no proposals; remove or list them. (6) Say that the Gini and Theil are population-weighted across 209-210 countries. (7) The proposal on regressing countries follows from the finding, but the 13.36% is a share of the assessed population, not of rural residents.

Numbers match their facts, with these exceptions. (1) Europe and Central Asia expected 2030 is 0.378, as the fact gives it, but the text also gives South Asia's value as 0.3782; both are correct. (2) The text gives the trend tool's 'Its ratio is 0.376' and the world rate is -0.03092, which is not cited; fine. (3) 'Each reported segment is slower than the one before' holds: -1.59231, -0.88, -0.325. (4) The 2025 reporting count of 4 is correct. Problems: the proposal to 'Direct acceleration effort' to the Middle East group and Sub-Saharan Africa does not follow cleanly from findings, since the data give no causes, and the proposal to fund a study of the 24 regression countries rests on a share (17.88 per cent) not tied to the proposal. The $1.25 line proposal presumes data that the bench does not have; qualify it. The 'Proposals' heading introduces a list the text itself does not show; put the proposals in the body. Where 'mean annual change' appears, add the unit (percentage points). The 2024 world value of 10.1 per cent rests on 26 reporting countries; say so in the finding itself.

Numbers: the population shares are rounded, so 3.8% (fact 0.0376), 4.4% (0.0436), 2.1% (0.0212) and 26.0% (0.2596) are acceptable roundings, but 'written as the result gives it' favours giving 3.76%, 4.36%, 2.12%, 25.96%. 26.0% is the one that reads as slightly off; use 26.0% only if rounding is stated. Other counts match. Findings: the convergence paragraph says 'dispersion widened', yet the heading and coefficient are fine; but 'the test gives no sign of catching up' infers direction the text admits is unknown. Cut or hedge that. The text also says 'Countries with high poverty by their own line tend to have high poverty by the international line': acceptable. The section does not answer how headcounts changed; state that plainly in the opening and shorten the repeated disclaimers. The 'Multidimensional' heading says 'comparable course', which overstates; the series differ (peak 2018 against 2021). Rename it. Remove the 'in at least one year' phrasing for 'any year' consistency.

Numbers match their facts, but several claims do not follow. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity is called 'the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale': meaningless; its 17.2-point gain exceeds every other region's, so say 'largest regional gain'. South Asia's expected 2030 electricity value (114.3542%) is omitted, though it is on track. (2) Rural sanitation: the text says no projection exists, true for the cited facts, but 'South Asia and Europe & Central Asia on track' for electricity and water are unmentioned; Europe & Central Asia is on track in electricity. (3) Sub-Saharan Africa water 'far below the target' is fine, but sanitation levels alone cannot show 'pace'; say so plainly. (4) The final heading 'Proposals follow from the gaps' ends on one line, and the proposals are not stated in the text; add them or cut the heading. (5) Cut 'fastest ... scale'; give the electricity world trend its expected 2030 value, 90.9205%. (6) Say rural sanitation Latin America and Middle East regions also lag.

### Displacement counts answer only part of the question

The question asks how many people were affected by disasters and what losses followed. The World Development Indicators supply one series that bears on it: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. No answer on losses is possible from this series, because it records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. It also counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income and cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced; this series speaks only to exposure, and only in the form of displacement cases.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because displacement depends heavily on the severity of the events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below, so the rise is reported with that caveat and is not a firm finding of worsening exposure.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023, the highest regional figures in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where displacing events grew, not who was displaced. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. In 2008 it was 80 and in 2009 it was 60. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.5701 in 2015 and 0.6783 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.7232 to 0.8935 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015 most of the unevenness came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share came from differences among countries within regions. A response designed only by region would therefore miss a growing part of the unevenness, though the sample change makes this a cautious reading.

Government expenditure on education, as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but five of the seven regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 16.9629% in 2015 to 15.3772% in 2024, a large drop from the highest starting share. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022, and Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024.

End years differ from 2022 to 2025, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical and comparisons between regions are indicative only. The count of 60 countries reporting in 2025 belongs to the education series as a whole, not to South Asia alone; it shows that the most recent endpoints rest on a thin base. A budget share is not an amount per child and does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. The data give no measure of need, so they show the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

(4) The text states 2023 as the last year of broad health coverage but 2024's 7 countries is a fact; fine. (5) The proposal on constant prices follows from the current-dollar caveat, but the finding about price effects is asserted, not shown by the data.

data.prompt: {"tool": "country-level-national-line-headcount-se", "need": "Country values of the national poverty headcount by year, with notes on revisions to national lines, to show direction and size of change.", "shelf examples": ["SH.DYN.MORT", "SI.POV.DDAY", "SP.POP.TOTL"]}

answer.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params['start_year'])
    y1 = int(params['end_year'])
    s = data[code]
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    rows = []
    for unit in s:
        for c in s[unit]:
            pass
    units = list(s.keys())
    unit = units[0] if units else ''
    ser = s[unit] if unit else {}
    changes = []
    for c in ser:
        if c not in regions:
            continue
        yrs = ser[c] if isinstance(ser[c], dict) else {}
        ys = sorted([int(y) for y in yrs if y0 <= int(y) <= y1])
        if len(ys) < 2:
            continue
        a = yrs[ys[0]] if ys[0] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[0])]
        b = yrs[ys[-1]] if ys[-1] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[-1])]
        changes.append((b - a, c, ys[0], ys[-1], a, b))
    changes.sort()
    n = len(changes)
    facts = {'series': code, 'unit': unit, 'countries_with_two_or_more_obs': n}
    if n == 0:
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'No country has two observations of ' + code + ' between ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + '; the change cannot be read.'}
    vals = [x[0] for x in changes]
    facts['median_change'] = round(statistics.median(vals), 2)
    facts['countries_falling'] = len([v for v in vals if v < 0])
    facts['countries_rising'] = len([v for v in vals if v > 0])
    best = changes[0]
    worst = changes[-1]
    facts['largest_fall_country'] = data['names'].get(best[1], best[1])
    facts['largest_fall'] = round(best[0], 2)
    facts['largest_rise_country'] = data['names'].get(worst[1], worst[1])
    facts['largest_rise'] = round(worst[0], 2)
    summary = ('Between first and last observations within ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ', ' + str(n) + ' countries report ' + code + ' (' + unit + '). The median change is ' + str(facts['median_change']) + '; ' + str(facts['countries_falling']) + ' fall and ' + str(facts['countries_rising']) + ' rise. The largest fall is in ' + facts['largest_fall_country'] + ' (' + str(facts['largest_fall']) + ' from ' + str(best[2]) + ' to ' + str(best[3]) + '). First and last years differ by country, and national lines are revised over time, so comparisons across years may reflect revised lines and not real change.')
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
answer.about: Computes, for each country, the change in a poverty or similar series between its first and last observation in a window, then reports the median change, counts of falling and rising countries and the extremes, with a caveat on revised national lines and uneven survey years.

params.name: series
params.meaning: World Bank series code to analyse, such as SI.POV.DDAY

params.name: start_year
params.meaning: First year of the window

params.name: end_year
params.meaning: Last year of the window

cases.expect: Facts list a positive count of countries with two or more observations, a negative median change in percentage points of population, more countries falling than rising, and a summary naming the largest fall with its years and the caveat on revised lines.
Under-five mortality per 1,000 live births falls in nearly all countries; the median change is clearly negative, countries_rising is near zero, and the summary states the unit and the largest fall.

answer.about: Summarises the latest coverage of all social protection and labour programmes for the poorest quintile (% of quintile population) per country within a year window, with extremes and regional medians. Reports missing data explicitly.

params.name: series
params.meaning: World Bank series code to analyse, e.g. per_allsp.cov_pop_tot or the poorest-quintile variant

params.name: year_from

cases.expect: facts include countries_with_data, median, mean, min, max, below_25, lowest and highest lists with years, and regional medians; values lie between 0 and 100 as percentages; summary states the median and range.

runs on a poverty series as a stand-in: facts give country count, median, extremes and three lowest and highest countries with years; if no data fall in the window the summary reports the series as missing.

They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3 countries. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 countries in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 countries in 2013. The results do not say why the count fell, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count fell: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

The spread of coverage (percentage of the poorest quintile) among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These years are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and the latest year with a reasonably large sample. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage; this is a hypothesis that the available results cannot test. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality falls

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a marked change. In 2015, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index. By 2018 the between-region share was 28.8 per cent, and by 2021 it was 21.4 per cent. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. In 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region. The change in sample composition between years makes it uncertain how much of this shift is real.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only 1 country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. carried.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params['start_year'])
    y1 = int(params['end_year'])
    s = data[code]
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    rows = []
    for unit in s:
        for c in s[unit]:
            pass
    units = list(s.keys())
    unit = units[0] if units else ''
    ser = s[unit] if unit else {}
    changes = []
    for c in ser:
        if c not in regions:
            continue
        yrs = ser[c] if isinstance(ser[c], dict) else {}
        ys = sorted([int(y) for y in yrs if y0 <= int(y) <= y1])
        if len(ys) < 2:
            continue
        a = yrs[ys[0]] if ys[0] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[0])]
        b = yrs[ys[-1]] if ys[-1] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[-1])]
        changes.append((b - a, c, ys[0], ys[-1], a, b))
    changes.sort()
    n = len(changes)
    facts = {'series': code, 'unit': unit, 'countries_with_two_or_more_obs': n}
    if n == 0:
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'No country has two observations of ' + code + ' between ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + '; the change cannot be read.'}
    vals = [x[0] for x in changes]
    facts['median_change'] = round(statistics.median(vals), 2)
    facts['countries_falling'] = len([v for v in vals if v < 0])
    facts['countries_rising'] = len([v for v in vals if v > 0])
    best = changes[0]
    worst = changes[-1]
    facts['largest_fall_country'] = data['names'].get(best[1], best[1])
    facts['largest_fall'] = round(best[0], 2)
    facts['largest_rise_country'] = data['names'].get(worst[1], worst[1])
    facts['largest_rise'] = round(worst[0], 2)
    summary = ('Between first and last observations within ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ', ' + str(n) + ' countries report ' + code + ' (' + unit + '). The median change is ' + str(facts['median_change']) + '; ' + str(facts['countries_falling']) + ' fall and ' + str(facts['countries_rising']) + ' rise. The largest fall is in ' + facts['largest_fall_country'] + ' (' + str(facts['largest_fall']) + ' from ' + str(best[2]) + ' to ' + str(best[3]) + '). First and last years differ by country, and national lines are revised over time, so comparisons across years may reflect revised lines and not real change.')
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

carried.comments: Most figures match their facts, but S1 and S3 have problems. (1) The 81 per cent and 39 per cent rises are not facts. They are flagged as calculated, which is honest, but S1 requires every number to be a fact, so cut them or state only the amounts. The claim that the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise depends on them. (2) The 60 countries reporting in 2025 is correctly matched to its fact, but its reading as showing a thin base is inference; say only that 60 countries reported. (3) The heading 'Education shares fell in most regions' is consistent with five of seven regions falling. Check that the count of five rests on mixed end years (2022 to 2025), and say so in the heading's paragraph. (4) The text states 2023 as the last year of broad health coverage but 2024's 7 countries is a fact; fine. (5) The proposal on constant prices follows from the current-dollar caveat, but the finding about price effects is asserted, not shown by the data.

Most figures match their facts, but several do not hold. (1) The claim that the 60 countries reporting in 2025 belong to the education series as a whole is not supported: fact c02-6.r1 gives 60 for 2025 with no series-wide scope, so attribute it carefully or cut the inference about a 'thin base'. (2) The percentages 81 and 39 are derived, not facts; they are flagged as such, but check them: 34.89/19.31 is about 80.7 per cent and 62.29/44.77 about 39.1 per cent, which is acceptable. (3) 'Five of the seven regions fell' is wrong on the figures: East Asia & Pacific, South Asia, North America, Sub-Saharan Africa and MENAAP fell, which is five, but the text lists seven regions while Europe & Central Asia is 'nearly flat', so state it plainly. (4) 'Aid rose in every region' needs North America excluded in the heading. (5) The 136 countries in 2023 and the 2024 count of 7 are fine. Name the 2022 end year for South Asia health consistently.

{"section": {"book": "Seventeen Goals, One Decade Left: A Global Analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015 to 2030, with Proposals", "chapter": "Goal 1: Poverty", "chapter kind": "goal", "section": "Disaster losses expose the vulnerable", "question": "How many people were affected by disasters and what losses followed?", "targets": [{"target": "1.5", "text": "By 2030, build the resilience of the poor and those in vulnerable situations and reduce their exposure and vulnerability to climate-related extreme events and other economic, social and environmental shocks and disasters"}]}, "regime": "peers", "version": {"text": "### Displacement counts answer only part of the question

The question asks how many people were affected by disasters and what losses followed. The World Development Indicators supply one series that bears on it: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. No answer on losses is possible from this series, because it records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. It also counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income and cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced; this series speaks only to exposure, and only in the form of displacement cases.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because displacement depends heavily on the severity of the events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below, so the rise is reported with that caveat and is not a firm finding of worsening exposure.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023, the highest regional figures in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where displacing events grew, not who was displaced. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. In 2008 it was 80 and in 2009 it was 60. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.5701 in 2015 and 0.6783 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.7232 to 0.8935 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015 most of the unevenness came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share came from differences among countries within regions. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They supply no global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and irregular

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013. The results do not say why, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. Among the years 2000 to 2023 the peak came in 2018, with 47 countries.

After 2018 the count was uneven rather than steadily falling: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023. Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion is lower in the smaller 2021 sample

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and a later year with 30 countries; 2022, with 17 countries, was too thin to use. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285, the Theil index 0.2032 and the coefficient of variation 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. The 2021 sample is smaller and the countries differ between years, so a narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

Decomposing the Theil index by region, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of it in 2015, 28.8 per cent in 2018 and 21.4 per cent in 2021. It also counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income and cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced; this series speaks only to exposure, and only in the form of displacement cases.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because displacement depends heavily on the severity of the events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below, so the rise is reported with that caveat and is not a firm finding of worsening exposure.

The Theil index rose from 0.7232 to 0.8935 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023.
